tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

entries.name: TaskStop
entries.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID ("name@team") or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

git commit -F - <<'EOF'
refactor(cdp): build the runtime over an attached Target session

RFC-03 requires a Step Run to hold one browser-level CDP connection with
one flattened Target session, and requires the run's CDPRuntime, and so
its frame manager, to sit on that session rather than on a page-level
WebSocket. The RFC states this as a contract requirement and specifies no
phasing for it. This is the first phase.

Before: `CDPHandler._connect_cdp` resolved a page-level WebSocket URL over
HTTP and opened `cdp_client.CDPClient` on it, sending with no `sessionId`.
After: it enters `one_shot_page_session` on an `AsyncExitStack` that lives
as long as the runtime, and wraps the result in `AttachedSessionClient`.

`AttachedSessionClient` presents the page-level client's surface over the
browser-level one. Threading a `session_id` through the handler instead
would touch about forty call sites across cdp_handler, frame_manager,
screencast, curated and interstitial in one change, with no intermediate
state that runs. Two behaviours are preserved deliberately, because
adopting the core client bare would drop both:

- The 30s command timeout. `core.cdp_client.CDPClient.send` awaits its
  future with no deadline, so a command Chrome never answers would hang.
- The exception type. cdp_handler and screencast both catch
  `cdp_client.CDPError`; the core client raises `core.errors.CDPError`
  and bare `ConnectionError`. Both are translated.

Target resolution is reused rather than reimplemented, so `--target 3` and
`--target B343DD76` keep meaning what they meant. `target_by` is derived
from the spec exactly as `cdp_client._resolve_among` derived it; the seam
rejects `None`, and a live run caught that before this landed.

`resolve_page_ws_url_async` lost its last caller here, so it goes.

Verified against a live browser: nineteen normalised transcript sections
across every handler-routed verb are identical on main and on this branch.
Per-invocation cost is flat, snapshot 98.7 -> 99.5 ms and frames list
93.9 -> 94.3 ms at the median, inside the run-to-run spread; the extra
Target.attachToTarget round trip is offset by dropping the HTTP lookup.
EOF
git log --oneline -1

gh pr create --title "refactor(cdp): build the runtime over an attached Target session" --body-file - <<'EOF'
RFC-03 Phase 1. The RFC requires a Step Run to hold one browser-level CDP
connection with one flattened `Target` session, and requires the run's
**CDPRuntime**, and therefore its frame manager, to sit on that session rather
than on a page-level WebSocket. RFC-03 states this as a requirement on the
contract and specifies no phasing for meeting it. This PR meets it, with no
new verb: the transport changes, the surface does not.

## What changed

`CDPHandler._connect_cdp` resolved a page-level WebSocket URL over HTTP and
opened `cdp_client.CDPClient` on it, sending with no `sessionId`. It now enters
`one_shot_page_session` on an `AsyncExitStack` held for the life of the
runtime, and wraps the result in the new `AttachedSessionClient`.

The exit stack rather than `async with` is the point: the session has to
outlive the one command that opened it, because a Step Run shares it across
every step.

## Why an adapter

Threading a `session_id` through the handler touches about forty call sites
across `cdp_handler`, `frame_manager`, `screencast`, `curated` and
`interstitial`, in one change, with no intermediate state that runs.
`AttachedSessionClient` presents the page-level client's surface over the
browser-level one instead, so the call sites do not move and the transport
under them does.

Two behaviours are preserved deliberately, because adopting the core client
bare would drop both:

- **The 30s command timeout.** `core.cdp_client.CDPClient.send` awaits its
  future with no deadline, so a command Chrome never answers hangs with no
  diagnostic. The page-level client always bounded it.
- **The exception type.** `cdp_handler` and `screencast` both catch
  `cdp_client.CDPError`. The core client raises `core.errors.CDPError`, an
  unrelated class, and a bare `ConnectionError`. Both are translated, so every
  existing `except CDPError` still fires.

## The bug the unit suite missed

`one_shot_page_session` dispatches on `target_by` and raises
`ValueError: Unknown target_by: None` when a spec arrives without one. The full
suite passed with `target_by=None` hardcoded; the live nine-verb comparison
caught it on `--target 1`. It is now derived exactly as
`cdp_client._resolve_among` derived it, and `TestTheTargetSpecIsTranslated`
pins the rule against the source it was copied from.

## Verification

- **Live behavioural comparison.** A harness drives every handler-routed verb
  against a real headless Chrome and prints a normalised transcript: navigate,
  snapshot, wait-idle, wait-stable, frames list/select/reset, storage get with
  and without `--key`, detect, click, fill, two fills from one snapshot (the v6
  UID rule), a stale UID after navigation, screencast, screenshot, and both
  target-resolution paths. **19 of 19 sections identical** on `main` and on this
  branch, including the two that must fail and their exact stderr.
- **Cost.** Median over 12 runs each, same machine, same page. `snapshot`
  98.7 -> 99.5 ms, `frames list` 93.9 -> 94.3 ms. Both inside the run-to-run
  spread already visible in the min/max columns. The extra
  `Target.attachToTarget` round trip is offset by dropping the HTTP page
  lookup.
- **Suite.** 1089 passed, 2 skipped. 20 of those are new, pinning the session
  on every send, the exception translation, the timeout bound, the session
  filter on subscriptions, and that the adapter never closes a socket it does
  not own.

## Also

`resolve_page_ws_url_async` lost its last caller here, so it is removed. The
sync `resolve_page_ws_url` stays; `test_stop_target.py` still covers it.

Not in this PR: the page-level `cdp_client.CDPClient` class now has no
production caller either, but it is re-exported from `browser_tools/__init__`
and shipped in 0.5.0. Removing it is a public-surface change and wants its own
PR.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

parts.text:
---
name: choose-model
description: "Pick the model for a piece of work from a deterministic registry: one command, a structured query in, an ordered list of routes (model through harness) out, each carrying what hcn needs to address it. Use before delegating to any subagent, worker, reviewer, or headless harness, or when asked which model should do a task. Not for running the delegation."
---

# Choose Model

Model routing is a lookup, not a judgment call. One command over
`references/registry.json` answers "which model, and which ones after
it" the same way every time. The unit it ranks is a **route**: a model
reached through one harness. The same model through two harnesses is
two routes, and they sit next to each other in the answer.

## When to query

Before any delegation where the model is not already pinned by the user
or by the calling skill's own spec: a subagent, a worker on another
harness, a reviewer (cross-family or not), a workflow stage, or the
question "which model should do X".

Skip it when a model is pinned, or when the work is a single edit
cheaper to make than to describe.

## The command

```bash
npx tsx <skill-dir>/scripts/choose.ts '<query-json>'   # or pipe JSON on stdin
npx tsx <skill-dir>/scripts/choose.ts --tasks          # task types
npx tsx <skill-dir>/scripts/choose.ts --models         # model and route facts
npx tsx <skill-dir>/scripts/choose.ts --matrix         # tables, for a human
```

`<skill-dir>` is the directory containing this loaded `SKILL.md`.
`--matrix` is for reading and for
explaining a decision after the fact. Never pick a model by reading the
matrix; that is the judgment call the query exists to replace.

## Query

```json
{ "task": "code-review", "stakes": "normal", "privacy": "normal",
  "needs": ["skills"], "excludeFamilies": ["glm"] }
```

- `task` (required): a registry task type; `--tasks` lists them.
- `stakes`: `low` | `normal` | `high` (default `normal`). Picks the
  minimums row. Low is throwaway; high is architecture-level or a
  user-facing hot path.
- `privacy`: `normal` | `secret` (default `normal`). `secret` means the
  prompt would carry secret material (credentials, tokens, `.env`
  contents, production output). Hosted routes are excluded outright.
- `needs`: extra capabilities beyond the task's own, e.g. `browser`,
  `desktop`, `skills`.
- `prefer`: `cost` | `speed` (default `cost`). `speed` ranks the routes
  that clear the minimums by measured response time, fastest first, with
  unmeasured routes last. Use it for quick lookups and exploration where
  waiting costs more than the call.
- `excludeFamilies`: hard exclusions. Pass the implementer's family when
  picking a reviewer so a model never reviews its own work.

## Building the query from a description

Writing `task` by hand is the judgment the registry exists to replace, and
`--tasks` is a list of eleven. When you have prose and not a query, build it:

```bash
npx tsx <skill-dir>/scripts/routing-query.ts --description <file> \
  [--stakes high] [--privacy secret] [--task implement] [--needs skills]
```

Out comes `query` (feed it straight to `choose.ts`) and `report`.

It asks four questions in one request and **decides only two fields**:

- **`task`**, when it is at least 0.85 confident. Below that the answer is
  still returned and `report.taskSource` says `jev-low-confidence`: supply
  `--task` yourself, or unattended take it and record that you did.
- **`needs`**, escalate-only. A high answer adds `browser` or `desktop`. A
  low one never removes a capability you asked for, because you know things
  the description does not carry.

**`stakes` and `privacy` are yours, always.** `stakes` is not asked at all;
it measured 58% and its confidence did not track its accuracy. `privacy` is
asked, recorded in `report.carriesSecret`, and gates nothing: three labelled
positives cannot set a threshold on a failure that leaks a credential. Set
`--privacy secret` yourself whenever the rule in GLOBAL.md applies.

The work description is the whole state, so its shape decides the answer.
Four rules govern it, and they were measured: applied to the five
descriptions the task question got wrong, the originals scored 0 of 5 and the
rewrites 4 of 5. Read
[references/work-description.md](references/work-description.md) before
writing one.

They fix the answer, not the confidence. Most recovered rows stay below the
act-band, so the caller still confirms the task. Shape rules do not buy
autonomy.

### When Jev does not answer

Routing keeps working. Only `MISSING_KEY` is fatal, because it is a setup
error and the message already names the wrapper that supplies the key.

Every other failure falls back to a **registry-chosen local route** that
decides `task` and the capability flags, and nothing else. `privacy` and
`stakes` take their safe values, `secret` and `high`, unless you stated them
yourself. The errors are asymmetric: a wrong `privacy` leaks a credential, a
wrong `task` wastes a run. The local route is never asked about privacy, so
there is no answer to be tempted by, and no uncalibrated number to mistake
for a band tuned on Jev's.

`report.fallback` records the code and the route, so an outage is visible in
the record instead of looking like a normal answer.

Two consequences to expect:

- **The query lands in the shortfall warning** for any task whose floor the
  local fleet cannot reach, because `privacy` is `secret`. That warning is
  written to read correctly here, where the cause is an outage rather than
  secret material.

# Delegate

Hand one piece of work to a worker model, from any harness, and report
who actually did it.

`<skill-dir>` is the directory containing this loaded `SKILL.md`; resolve
bundled commands from there, regardless of the target project directory.

## Preconditions

Every Jev-backed script here (`question-gate.ts`, `brief-gate.ts`,
`verify-result.ts`, `routing-query.ts`) needs `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in its
environment. The key is injected, never read from a file, so a bare `npx tsx`
call exits 1 with `TYPESAFE_API_KEY is not set`. Wrap the call in `opchain`,
which resolves the reference in `~/.agents/secrets/jev.env.op` into that one
child process and writes nothing back. Every gate command below is shown
wrapped.

- [choose-model](../choose-model/SKILL.md) and the `hcn` binary
  (`npm install -g @dungle-scrubs/harness-cli-normalizer`). No other path
  substitutes for hcn: a hand-built `codex exec` or `pi -p` call is how
  delegations fail silently.
- No subagent tool: treat every route as cross-harness and run it
  through the script.
- No human: a `question` report takes its `recommended` answer, records
  the decision as machine-made where the work's decisions live, and
  resumes within the caller's existing authority for reversible work. Shared
  writes and decisions requiring missing authority wait for the human.

  Put that reading to the gate rather than making it yourself:

  ```bash
  opchain primary --read op run --env-file="$HOME/.agents/secrets/jev.env.op" -- \
    npx tsx <skill-dir>/scripts/question-gate.ts --input question.json
  ```

  Two Nouls over the brief, the question and the recommendation. It **detects
  rather than authorises**: a high `writes_shared_surface` stops the
  auto-take, and a low one authorises nothing on its own. The only case that
  proceeds is reversible **and** private, both established. No answer waits,
  the same as a cautious answer. Exits 2 when the recommendation must wait.

   shape and the verification bar for the result are yours to decide per

cat > /Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/.scratch/rfc-03-phase1/brief.md <<'EOF'
# Adversarial review: converge CDPRuntime onto an attached Target session

You are reviewing a merged-pending change in a Python CLI. Read the sources
yourself; nothing is pasted here.

## Where

Repository: `/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools`
Branch under review: `feat/handler-over-attached-session`
Base: `main`
Pull request: https://github.com/dungle-scrubs/browser-tools/pull/126

The whole change is one commit. Read it with:

```
cd /Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools
git log --oneline main..feat/handler-over-attached-session
git diff main...feat/handler-over-attached-session
```

You have read access to the working tree. Do not edit any file, do not
commit, do not push, do not comment on the PR. Produce a report only.

## What the product is

`bt` is a CLI that drives Chrome and Camoufox over the Chrome DevTools
Protocol. Read `CONTEXT.md` first: it is the naming authority, and the nouns
**One-Shot Session**, **CDPRuntime**, **UID**, **Bounded Capture** and **The
Manual** all bear on this change.

Every `bt` invocation is a separate OS process that opens a CDP connection,
does its work, and exits. Nothing outlives the invocation.

## What the change does

Two CDP clients exist in this codebase and they are not interchangeable:

- `src/browser_tools/cdp_client.py` opens a **page-level** WebSocket, sends
  with no `sessionId`, and registers event handlers with no session filter.
- `src/browser_tools/core/cdp_client.py` opens a **browser-level** WebSocket
  and carries a `sessionId` on every send and every event.

`CDPHandler` / `CDPRuntime` in `src/browser_tools/cdp_handler.py` used the
first. This change moves it to the second, via `one_shot_page_session` in
`src/browser_tools/one_shot.py` and a new adapter,
`src/browser_tools/attached_session.py`.

New tests are in `tests/test_attached_session.py`.

## Why

`docs/rfc/03_*.rfc.md` specifies a Step Run: one invocation, one CDP
connection, one attached session, many steps. It requires the run's
CDPRuntime, and therefore its frame manager, to be built over that attached
session. Read the RFC, in particular the section stating that requirement and
the note that it specifies no phasing. This PR is the first phase and adds no
verb.

## What to attack

Rank by what would actually break a user. For each finding give the concrete
input or state, the wrong behaviour, and the file and line.

1. **Event dispatch.** `core/cdp_client.py` dispatches an event to a callback
   only when the callback's filter session is `None` or equals the event's
   `sessionId`. Find every place the handler, the frame manager, the
   screencast state machine, `curated.py` and `interstitial.py` subscribe to
   or wait on a CDP event. Does each one still receive what it received on a
   page-level connection? Pay attention to events that arrive on the
   **browser** session or on a **different** target's session rather than on
   the attached page session: `Target.*`, and anything from an out-of-process
   iframe or a popup. An event that silently stops arriving is the failure
   mode this change most plausibly introduces, and the test suite would not
   see it.

2. **Lifetime and teardown order.** `CDPRuntime._main` now holds an
   `AsyncExitStack`. Check the ordering against the old code: what is closed
   first, what happens if `_connect_cdp` raises partway, what happens if the
   browser dies mid-run, what happens if `_main` is cancelled. The stack's
   `aclose` is wrapped in `contextlib.suppress(Exception)` - argue whether
   that hides a failure a caller needed to see.

3. **The adapter's fidelity.** `AttachedSessionClient` is supposed to present
   `cdp_client.CDPClient`'s surface. Compare the two side by side. Any method,
   attribute or property a caller uses that the adapter does not provide is a
   runtime `AttributeError`. Check `connected`, `send`, `on`, `off`,
   `disconnect`, and anything else callers touch. Note that `connected` reads
   a private `_connected` attribute off the core client via `getattr`.

4. **Timeout semantics.** The adapter re-applies a 30s bound with
   `asyncio.wait_for` because the core client's `send` awaits with no
   deadline. On timeout the core client keeps the pending future and its
   entry in whatever pending-request map it holds. Read
   `core/cdp_client.py` and say whether that leaks, and whether a later
   response for the abandoned id can be misrouted or crash the reader task.

5. **Exception translation.** The adapter catches `core.errors.CDPError`,
   `TimeoutError` and `ConnectionError` and re-raises
   `cdp_client.CDPError`. Find any other exception type the core client or
   the websockets library can raise out of `send` that a caller used to
   receive as `CDPError` and now would not. `asyncio.CancelledError` deserves
   specific attention: `wait_for` and `BaseException` inheritance interact
   here.

6. **Target resolution.** The old path used
   `cdp_client.resolve_page_ws_url` / `_resolve_among`. The new path uses
   `one_shot_page_session` -> `core/attach.py:resolve_target`. Read both and
   say whether `--target N` selects the same page. Specifically: what each
   one treats as the candidate list, in what order it sorts, and whether both
   filter to page targets the same way. A silent change of which page
   `--target 1` means would be a serious regression, and the author asserts
   the orderings match.

7. **Error surface.** Run the change's failure paths in your head. When the

    async def send(
        self, method: str, params: dict[str, Any] | None = None, timeout: float | None = None
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Send a CDP command and wait for the response.

        Args:
            method: CDP method name (e.g., "Page.getFrameTree").
            params: Method parameters.
            timeout: Override default timeout for this call.

        Returns:
            CDP response result dictionary.

        Raises:
            CDPError: If the command fails or times out.
        """
        if not self._ws or not self._connected:
            raise CDPError("Not connected to Chrome CDP")

        self._msg_id += 1
        msg_id = self._msg_id
        message: dict[str, Any] = {"id": msg_id, "method": method}
        if params:
            message["params"] = params

        future: asyncio.Future[dict[str, Any]] = asyncio.get_event_loop().create_future()
        self._pending[msg_id] = future

        try:
            await self._ws.send(json.dumps(message))
        except (OSError, TypeError, asyncio.CancelledError) as exc:
            self._pending.pop(msg_id, None)
            raise CDPError(f"Failed to send CDP command: {exc}") from exc

        effective_timeout = timeout if timeout is not None else self._timeout
        try:
            response = await asyncio.wait_for(future, timeout=effective_timeout)
        except TimeoutError as exc:
            self._pending.pop(msg_id, None)
            raise CDPError(f"CDP command timed out after {effective_timeout}s: {method}") from exc

        if "error" in response:
            raise CDPError(
                f"CDP error in {method}: {response['error'].get('message', response['error'])}"
            )
        return response.get("result", {})

Confirmed a regression I introduced. The page-level client popped its pending entry on timeout (`cdp_client.py:151`); my adapter wraps the whole coroutine, so it cannot. Consequences in `core/cdp_client.py`:

- the `_pending` entry leaks for the life of the connection
- a late response finds it at line 145, calls `set_result` on the future `wait_for` already cancelled, raises `InvalidStateError`, which the `except Exception` at line 165 catches by **killing the receive loop** - the whole connection dies

Under a Step Run that is one timed-out step taking the rest of the run with it. Fixing it at the source.

"""The handler's client, backed by an attached Target session.

RFC-03 requires a Step Run to hold one browser-level CDP connection with one
flattened ``Target`` session, and requires the run's **CDPRuntime, and
therefore its frame manager, to be built over that attached session** rather
than over a page-level WebSocket. That is a change to how ``CDPHandler``
connects, and the RFC states it as a contract requirement without phasing.
This module is the first phase of meeting it.

Why an adapter rather than a rewrite
------------------------------------
Two clients exist and they are not interchangeable:

- ``cdp_client.CDPClient`` opens a **page-level** socket, sends with no
  ``sessionId``, and registers event handlers with no session filter. The
  handler and everything under it use this one.
- ``core.cdp_client.CDPClient`` opens a **browser-level** socket and carries a
  ``sessionId`` on every send and every event. ``one_shot_page_session`` uses
  this one.

The difference is not cosmetic. ``core/cdp_client.py`` dispatches an event to
a callback only when the callback's filter session is ``None`` or equal to the
event's ``sessionId``, so a page-level connection and a session-filtered
subscriber never meet.

Converging them by threading a ``session_id`` through the handler would touch
about forty call sites across ``cdp_handler``, ``frame_manager``,
``screencast``, ``curated`` and ``interstitial``, in one change, with no
intermediate state that runs. This class instead presents the page-level
client's surface over the browser-level one, so the call sites do not move and
the transport underneath them does. What each caller sends is unchanged; where
it is sent changes.

What this preserves deliberately
--------------------------------
- **The command timeout.** ``core.cdp_client.CDPClient.send`` awaits its
  future with no deadline, so a command Chrome never answers hangs forever.
  The page-level client bounds every command at 30 seconds. Adopting the core
  client without this wrapper would silently drop that bound, so ``send``
  re-applies it here.
- **The exception type.** ``cdp_handler`` and ``screencast`` both catch
  ``cdp_client.CDPError``. The core client raises ``core.errors.CDPError``,
  an unrelated class, and a ``ConnectionError`` when the socket is gone. Both
  are translated, so every existing ``except CDPError`` still fires.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import logging
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Any

from .cdp_client import CDPError
from .core.errors import CDPError as CoreCDPError

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from .core.cdp_client import CDPClient as CoreCDPClient

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

#: Matches ``cdp_client.CDPClient``'s default. A command that never returns is
#: a hung invocation, and the page-level client has always bounded it.
DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 30.0


class AttachedSessionClient:
    """``cdp_client.CDPClient``'s surface over one attached Target session.

    Wraps a connected ``core.cdp_client.CDPClient`` and the ``sessionId`` of a
    flattened ``Target`` session on it. Every send carries that session, and
    every event subscription filters on it.

    The lifetime of the connection and the session belongs to whoever opened
    them, which is ``one_shot_page_session``. This object never closes either.
    """

    def __init__(self, client: CoreCDPClient, session_id: str) -> None:
        self._client = client
        self._session_id = session_id
        self._closed = False

    @property
    def session_id(self) -> str:
        """The attached session every send and subscription carries."""
        return self._session_id

    @property
    def connected(self) -> bool:
        """Whether the underlying connection is usable.

        ``CDPHandler.available`` reads this, and ``curated`` polls that to
        decide the handler came up, so it has to mean the same thing it did
        on the page-level client.
        """
        return not self._closed and bool(getattr(self._client, "_connected", False))

    async def send(
        self,
        method: str,
        params: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
        timeout: float | None = None,
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Send one command over the attached session and return its result.

        Signature and return shape match ``cdp_client.CDPClient.send``, so the
        call sites do not change. ``CDPError`` is raised for a protocol error,
        a lost connection, and a timeout, because that is the one exception
        those call sites catch.
        """
        if self._closed:
            raise CDPError("Not connected to Chrome CDP")
        deadline = DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS if timeout is None else timeout
        try:
            return await asyncio.wait_for(
                self._client.send(method=method, params=params, session_id=self._session_id),
                timeout=deadline,
            )
        except CoreCDPError as exc:
            raise CDPError(f"CDP error in {method}: {exc.message}") from exc
        except TimeoutError as exc:
            # The core client keeps the pending future; the session is torn
            # down at the end of the invocation, which collects it.
            raise CDPError(f"CDP command timed out after {deadline}s: {method}") from exc
        except ConnectionError as exc:
            raise CDPError(f"Failed to send CDP command: {exc}") from exc

    def on(self, event: str, handler: Any) -> None:
        """Subscribe to an event on this session only.

        The session filter is the whole point: without it a subscriber on a
        browser-level connection would also see the same event from every
        other attached target.
        """
        self._client.on(event, handler, session_id=self._session_id)

    def off(self, event: str, handler: Any) -> None:
        """Unsubscribe. A handler that was never registered is ignored."""
        self._client.off(event, handler)

    async def disconnect(self) -> None:
        """Mark this client unusable without touching the connection.

        The connection and the session are owned by the context manager that
        opened them. Closing them here would detach a session that manager is
        about to detach again, and close a socket it still holds.
        """
        self._closed = True

"""A wait that ends early must not leave the connection poisoned.

``core.cdp_client.CDPClient`` keeps one ``_pending`` entry per in-flight
command and one receive loop for the whole connection. When a waiter goes
away before Chrome answers - a timeout, a cancellation - the entry it left
behind is still there when the late response arrives. The loop finds it,
delivers to a future nobody holds, and ``InvalidStateError`` reaches its own
``except Exception``, which answers by returning. That kills the receive
loop, and with it every command on that connection.

It matters more than it used to. A page-level connection lived for one
command. RFC-03's Step Run shares one connection across every step, so one
step that times out would take the rest of the run with it.

These tests drive the real ``send`` and the real ``_recv_loop``.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import json

import pytest

from browser_tools.core.cdp_client import CDPClient

_STOP = object()


class ControllableWebSocket:
    """A websocket that answers only what the test decides to answer.

    Async-iterable, so the real ``_recv_loop`` consumes it unchanged.
    """

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.sent: list[dict] = []
        self._inbox: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue()

    async def send(self, raw: str) -> None:
        self.sent.append(json.loads(raw))

1	"""A wait that ends early must not leave the connection poisoned.
2	
3	``core.cdp_client.CDPClient`` keeps one ``_pending`` entry per in-flight
4	command and one receive loop for the whole connection. When a waiter goes
5	away before Chrome answers - a timeout, a cancellation - the entry it left
6	behind is still there when the late response arrives. The loop finds it,
7	delivers to a future nobody holds, and ``InvalidStateError`` reaches its own
8	``except Exception``, which answers by returning. That kills the receive
9	loop, and with it every command on that connection.
10	
11	It matters more than it used to. A page-level connection lived for one
12	command. RFC-03's Step Run shares one connection across every step, so one
13	step that times out would take the rest of the run with it.
14	
15	These tests drive the real ``send`` and the real ``_recv_loop``.
16	"""
17	
18	from __future__ import annotations
19	
20	import asyncio
21	import json

24	import pytest_asyncio

git add src/browser_tools/core/cdp_client.py src/browser_tools/attached_session.py tests/test_attached_session.py tests/test_core_send_timeout.py && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
fix(cdp): retire a pending command when its waiter gives up

Self-review of the transport change found a regression it introduced.

The page-level client bounded every command at 30s and popped its own
`_pending` entry when the bound elapsed, because the bound lived inside
`send` where `msg_id` is in scope. The adapter re-applied the bound with an
`asyncio.wait_for` around `core.cdp_client.CDPClient.send`, which cannot
reach `msg_id`, so the entry stayed.

Two things follow, and the second is the serious one:

- The entry leaks for the life of the connection.
- The late response finds it. `_recv_loop` pops it and calls `set_result` on
  a future `wait_for` already cancelled. `InvalidStateError` reaches the
  loop's own `except Exception`, which answers by returning. The receive
  loop dies and every later command on that connection fails.

That was survivable when a connection served one command. RFC-03's Step Run
shares one connection across every step, so one step that timed out would
have taken the rest of the run with it.

The bound moves into `core.cdp_client.CDPClient.send`, which retires the
entry on both a timeout and a cancellation. `_recv_loop` also drops a
message whose future is already done, covering a future cancelled where the
client cannot see it. The adapter passes its 30s down instead of wrapping.

`send`'s default stays no-bound, so every existing One-Shot Session caller
is unchanged.

Both fixes are load-bearing: with the receive-loop guard removed, 2 of the
10 new tests fail; with the retirement removed, a different 2 fail; with
neither, 7 fail.

Suite 1100 passed, 2 skipped. The live nine-verb comparison against main is
unchanged: 16 sections identical, 2 differing only in a measured
millisecond count, and the bad-target case differing only in traceback
frames, with the same TargetNotFoundError, the same message, the same
`error:` line and the same exit 1.
EOF
git log --oneline -2

gh pr edit 126 --body-file - <<'EOF'
RFC-03 Phase 1. The RFC requires a Step Run to hold one browser-level CDP
connection with one flattened `Target` session, and requires the run's
**CDPRuntime**, and therefore its frame manager, to sit on that session rather
than on a page-level WebSocket. RFC-03 states this as a requirement on the
contract and specifies no phasing for meeting it. This PR meets it, with no
new verb: the transport changes, the surface does not.

Two commits. The first makes the change; the second fixes a regression the
first introduced, which self-review found before merge.

## 1. The transport change

`CDPHandler._connect_cdp` resolved a page-level WebSocket URL over HTTP and
opened `cdp_client.CDPClient` on it, sending with no `sessionId`. It now enters
`one_shot_page_session` on an `AsyncExitStack` held for the life of the
runtime, and wraps the result in the new `AttachedSessionClient`.

The exit stack rather than `async with` is the point: the session has to
outlive the one command that opened it, because a Step Run shares it across
every step.

### Why an adapter

Threading a `session_id` through the handler touches about forty call sites
across `cdp_handler`, `frame_manager`, `screencast`, `curated` and
`interstitial`, in one change, with no intermediate state that runs.
`AttachedSessionClient` presents the page-level client's surface over the
browser-level one instead, so the call sites do not move and the transport
under them does.

Two behaviours are preserved deliberately, because adopting the core client
bare would drop both:

- **The 30s command timeout.** `core.cdp_client.CDPClient.send` defaulted to
  no deadline, so a command Chrome never answers hangs with no diagnostic. The
  page-level client always bounded it.
- **The exception type.** `cdp_handler` and `screencast` both catch
  `cdp_client.CDPError`. The core client raises `core.errors.CDPError`, an
  unrelated class, and a bare `ConnectionError`. Both are translated, so every
  existing `except CDPError` still fires.

### The bug the unit suite missed

`one_shot_page_session` dispatches on `target_by` and raises
`ValueError: Unknown target_by: None` when a spec arrives without one. The full
suite passed with `target_by=None` hardcoded; the live nine-verb comparison
caught it on `--target 1`. It is now derived exactly as
`cdp_client._resolve_among` derived it, and `TestTheTargetSpecIsTranslated`
pins the rule against the source it was copied from.

## 2. The regression the first commit introduced

The page-level client's 30s bound lived inside `send`, where `msg_id` is in
scope, so a timeout popped its own `_pending` entry. The adapter re-applied the
bound with an `asyncio.wait_for` **around** `core.cdp_client.CDPClient.send`,
which cannot reach `msg_id`. The entry stayed.

Two things follow, and the second is the serious one:

- The entry leaks for the life of the connection.
- The late response finds it. `_recv_loop` pops it and calls `set_result` on a
  future `wait_for` already cancelled. `InvalidStateError` reaches the loop's
  own `except Exception`, which answers by returning. **The receive loop dies
  and every later command on that connection fails.**

Survivable when a connection served one command. Under a Step Run sharing one
connection across every step, one step that times out takes the rest of the
run with it.

The fix moves the bound into `core.cdp_client.CDPClient.send`, which retires
the entry on both a timeout and a cancellation. `_recv_loop` also drops a
message whose future is already done, covering a future cancelled where the
client cannot see it. The adapter passes its 30s down instead of wrapping.

`send`'s default stays no-bound, so every existing One-Shot Session caller is
unchanged.

## Verification

- **Live behavioural comparison.** A harness drives every handler-routed verb
  against a real headless Chrome and prints a normalised transcript: navigate,
  snapshot, wait-idle, wait-stable, frames list/select/reset, storage get with
  and without `--key`, detect, click, fill, two fills from one snapshot (the v6
  UID rule), a stale UID after navigation, screencast, screenshot, and both
  target-resolution paths.

  19 sections. 16 identical byte for byte. 2 differ only in a measured
  millisecond count (`idle after 505ms` vs `509ms`). 1 is the bad-target
  failure, where the intermediate traceback frames differ because the code
  changed, and the `TargetNotFoundError`, its message
  (`Index 99 out of range (1-1)`), the `error:` line and exit 1 are all
  identical. Both paths raise from `core.attach`, which is independent
  evidence that target resolution is unchanged.

- **Mutation check on the fix.** Removing the receive-loop guard fails 2 of
  the 10 new core tests; removing the retirement fails a different 2; removing
  both fails 7. Each fix is independently load-bearing.

- **Cost.** Median over 12 runs each, same machine, same page. `snapshot`
  98.7 -> 99.5 ms, `frames list` 93.9 -> 94.3 ms. Both inside the run-to-run
  spread already visible in the min/max columns. The extra
  `Target.attachToTarget` round trip is offset by dropping the HTTP page
  lookup.

- **Suite.** 1100 passed, 2 skipped. 31 are new.

## Also

`resolve_page_ws_url_async` lost its last caller here, so it is removed. The
sync `resolve_page_ws_url` stays; `test_stop_target.py` still covers it.

Two things deliberately not in this PR:

- The page-level `cdp_client.CDPClient` class now has no production caller
  either, but it is re-exported from `browser_tools/__init__` and shipped in
  0.5.0. Removing it is a public-surface change and wants its own PR.
- A failed CDP connection prints a full traceback to stderr before the
  one-line `error:`. That is pre-existing, identical on `main`, and worth its
  own fix.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

connection with one flattened `Target` session, and requires the run's
**CDPRuntime**, and therefore its frame manager, to sit on that session rather
than on a page-level WebSocket. RFC-03 states this as a requirement on the
contract and specifies no phasing for meeting it. This PR meets it, with no
new verb: the transport changes, the surface does not.

Two commits. The first makes the change; the second fixes a regression the
first introduced, which self-review found before merge.

## 1. The transport change

`CDPHandler._connect_cdp` resolved a page-level WebSocket URL over HTTP and
opened `cdp_client.CDPClient` on it, sending with no `sessionId`. It now enters
`one_shot_page_session` on an `AsyncExitStack` held for the life of the
runtime, and wraps the result in the new `AttachedSessionClient`.

The exit stack rather than `async with` is the point: the session has to
outlive the one command that opened it, because a Step Run shares it across
every step.

### Why an adapter

Threading a `session_id` through the handler touches about forty call sites
across `cdp_handler`, `frame_manager`, `screencast`, `curated` and
`interstitial`, in one change, with no intermediate state that runs.
`AttachedSessionClient` presents the page-level client's surface over the
browser-level one instead, so the call sites do not move and the transport
under them does.

Two behaviours are preserved deliberately, because adopting the core client
bare would drop both:

- **The 30s command timeout.** `core.cdp_client.CDPClient.send` defaulted to
  no deadline, so a command Chrome never answers hangs with no diagnostic. The
  page-level client always bounded it.
- **The exception type.** `cdp_handler` and `screencast` both catch
  `cdp_client.CDPError`. The core client raises `core.errors.CDPError`, an
  unrelated class, and a bare `ConnectionError`. Both are translated, so every
  existing `except CDPError` still fires.

### The bug the unit suite missed

`one_shot_page_session` dispatches on `target_by` and raises
`ValueError: Unknown target_by: None` when a spec arrives without one. The full
suite passed with `target_by=None` hardcoded; the live nine-verb comparison
caught it on `--target 1`. It is now derived exactly as
`cdp_client._resolve_among` derived it, and `TestTheTargetSpecIsTranslated`
pins the rule against the source it was copied from.

## 2. The regression the first commit introduced

The page-level client's 30s bound lived inside `send`, where `msg_id` is in
scope, so a timeout popped its own `_pending` entry. The adapter re-applied the
bound with an `asyncio.wait_for` **around** `core.cdp_client.CDPClient.send`,
which cannot reach `msg_id`. The entry stayed.

Two things follow, and the second is the serious one:

- The entry leaks for the life of the connection.
- The late response finds it. `_recv_loop` pops it and calls `set_result` on a
  future `wait_for` already cancelled. `InvalidStateError` reaches the loop's
  own `except Exception`, which answers by returning. **The receive loop dies
  and every later command on that connection fails.**

Survivable when a connection served one command. Under a Step Run sharing one
connection across every step, one step that times out takes the rest of the
run with it.

The fix moves the bound into `core.cdp_client.CDPClient.send`, which retires
the entry on both a timeout and a cancellation. `_recv_loop` also drops a
message whose future is already done, covering a future cancelled where the
client cannot see it. The adapter passes its 30s down instead of wrapping.

`send`'s default stays no-bound, so every existing One-Shot Session caller is
unchanged.

## Verification

- **Live behavioural comparison.** A harness drives every handler-routed verb
  against a real headless Chrome and prints a normalised transcript: navigate,
  snapshot, wait-idle, wait-stable, frames list/select/reset, storage get with
  and without `--key`, detect, click, fill, two fills from one snapshot (the v6
  UID rule), a stale UID after navigation, screencast, screenshot, and both
  target-resolution paths.

  19 sections. 16 identical byte for byte. 2 differ only in a measured
  millisecond count (`idle after 505ms` vs `509ms`). 1 is the bad-target
  failure, where the intermediate traceback frames differ because the code
  changed, and the `TargetNotFoundError`, its message
  (`Index 99 out of range (1-1)`), the `error:` line and exit 1 are all
  identical. Both paths raise from `core.attach`, which is independent
  evidence that target resolution is unchanged.

- **Mutation check on the fix.** Removing the receive-loop guard fails 2 of
  the 10 new core tests; removing the retirement fails a different 2; removing
  both fails 7. Each fix is independently load-bearing.

- **Cost.** Median over 12 runs each, same machine, same page. `snapshot`
  98.7 -> 99.5 ms, `frames list` 93.9 -> 94.3 ms. Both inside the run-to-run
  spread already visible in the min/max columns. The extra
  `Target.attachToTarget` round trip is offset by dropping the HTTP page
  lookup.

- **Suite.** 1100 passed, 2 skipped. 31 are new.

## Also

`resolve_page_ws_url_async` lost its last caller here, so it is removed. The
sync `resolve_page_ws_url` stays; `test_stop_target.py` still covers it.

Two things deliberately not in this PR:

- The page-level `cdp_client.CDPClient` class now has no production caller
  either, but it is re-exported from `browser_tools/__init__` and shipped in
  0.5.0. Removing it is a public-surface change and wants its own PR.
- A failed CDP connection prints a full traceback to stderr before the
  one-line `error:`. That is pre-existing, identical on `main`, and worth its
  own fix.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

Review of commit `54de3ff`: **three blocking findings**.

I could not write `/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/.scratch/rfc-03-phase1/review-gpt6.md` because this session permits filesystem reads only. The report follows. No files were changed by this review.

The working tree changed during the review. All findings below refer to the committed revision, excluding those concurrent edits. I accepted the supplied test, live-comparison, and timing results without rerunning them. Additional verification used in-memory transport fixtures and CLI calls with mocked discovery, not live Chrome.

**Blocking**

1. **Omitting `--target` now fails when several pages exist.**

   **Location:** `src/browser_tools/cdp_handler.py:444`.

   **Trigger:** Run `bt INSTANCE frames list` with two page targets. A popup left open creates the same condition.

   **Wrong behaviour:** The old resolver selects the first page sorted by target ID when the spec is `None` (`cdp_client.py:280`). The new path passes `None` to `resolve_target`, which raises `AmbiguousTargetError` for several pages (`core/attach.py:127`). After the connection wait, the CLI reports that it could not open a CDP session.

   This affects more than commands where users can add `--target`. `frames`, `storage`, semantic waits, `detect`, and `screencast` do not expose that escape route.

   **Fix:** Preserve the handler's existing default by passing `"1"` with `"index"` when its target spec is absent. Keep the One-Shot Session's existing ambiguity policy for its other callers.

   **Evidence:** Resolver probes confirmed the old default selected `AAA`; the new default raised `AmbiguousTargetError`. A mocked-discovery `frames list` invocation returned exit 1 with empty stdout.

2. **A late response after timeout stops the reader and fails unrelated pending commands.**

   **Location:** `src/browser_tools/attached_session.py:114`; underlying delivery at `src/browser_tools/core/cdp_client.py:145`.

   **Trigger:** A CDP command exceeds its deadline, then Chrome returns its response while the invocation remains active. Cancellation of an outstanding screencast acknowledgement can create the same cancelled-future state.

   **Wrong behaviour:** `wait_for` cancels the core send and its awaited future. The core retains that future in `_pending`. When the response arrives, the reader calls `set_result` or `set_exception` on the cancelled future. This raises `InvalidStateError`, ends the receive loop, marks the connection disconnected, and fails other pending requests.

   The comment at `attached_session.py:121` treats this as temporary retention until teardown. It is also a connection failure. Python explicitly rejects setting a result on a completed or cancelled future. [Python Future contract](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-future.html#asyncio.Future.set_result)

   **Fix:** Make request cancellation remove the abandoned request entry and make response delivery ignore completed futures. Respect the vendoring restriction: implement the repair in a maintained transport adaptation or obtain an approved upstream refresh.

   **Evidence:** The actual committed core client retained one cancelled future after timeout. Delivering its late response logged `invalid state`, stopped the reader, and failed a second command with `CDPError`.

3. **Ordinary discovery failures now print tracebacks.**

   **Location:** `src/browser_tools/cdp_handler.py:444`, reaching the existing exception logger at line 470.

   **Trigger:** The browser exits before discovery, the port is wrong, or the endpoint has no page targets.

   **Wrong behaviour:** The old HTTP resolver returned `None` for unavailable endpoints or no pages. The new One-Shot Session raises. `_connect_cdp` logs that exception with a traceback, discards its specific cause, and leaves `curated` waiting until its connection deadline. The CLI then prints its generic error.

   Exit 1 and empty stdout survive. The requested clean stderr contract does not. Explicit unmatched and ambiguous target specs also reach this logger, although those traceback paths already existed before this commit.

   **Fix:** Store expected startup failures on CDPRuntime and propagate them promptly through `_cdp_handler_session` as `LifecycleError`. Reserve traceback logging for unexpected defects.

   **Evidence:** Mocked-discovery CLI probes for an unavailable browser, multiple pages, and an unmatched target all returned exit 1, empty stdout, and a traceback before the final diagnostic.

**Non-blocking**

1. **`off()` does not remove the screencast's bound-method callback.**

   **Location:** `src/browser_tools/attached_session.py:138`.

   **Trigger:** `ScreencastRecorder.start()` subscribes with `self.on_frame`; `stop()` or failed-start cleanup unsubscribes with a fresh access to `self.on_frame`.

   **Wrong behaviour:** The old client removes callbacks by equality. The core removes them by identity. Those bound-method objects compare equal but are not identical, so the subscription remains. One Bounded Capture is mostly protected by `_active = False` and process exit. Reusing the recorder would accumulate callbacks and duplicate frames and acknowledgements.

   **Fix:** Retain the exact registered callback in the adapter and use it for removal, preserving the old matching semantics.

   **Evidence:** The committed adapter retained one callback after removal; the old client retained zero.

2. **Cancelling `_main` skips the new stack's cleanup.**

   **Location:** `src/browser_tools/cdp_handler.py:391`.

   **Trigger:** Cancel `_main` while it awaits `_stop_event`, or after successful session entry during initialization.

   **Wrong behaviour:** `AsyncExitStack` is neither entered with `async with` nor closed in `finally`. Cancellation bypasses lines 402-408, leaving explicit detach and close undone. The old runtime also lacked cancellation-safe cleanup; this change retains that defect for its new resource owner. Normal CLI shutdown signals the stop event, so this is not its usual path.

   **Fix:** Put initialization and the stop wait inside the stack's context or a `try/finally`. Complete cleanup before propagating cancellation. `CancelledError` inherits from `BaseException`, so `suppress(Exception)` does not catch it. [Python cancellation guidance](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html#task-cancellation)

   **Evidence:** Cancelling the committed `_main` left a registered stack cleanup callback uncalled.

3. **The target-translation tests do not exercise target translation.**

   **Location:** `tests/test_attached_session.py:196`.

   **Trigger:** Remove or break the translation in `_connect_cdp`.

   **Wrong behaviour:** The test still passes because it calculates its own copy of the expression. The next test searches the old resolver's source text. Neither observes what CDPRuntime passes to the One-Shot Session.

   **Fix:** Invoke runtime initialization with an instrumented session seam. Assert the arguments received for omitted, numeric, and ID-prefix specs. Include multiple pages for the omitted case.

4. **The added comments repeat implementation and migration history.**

   **Locations:** `attached_session.py:3`, `:61`, `:90`, `:121`, `:130`, `:143`; `cdp_handler.py:322`, `:404`, `:413`, `:436`.

   **Trigger:** A maintainer reads these sections to determine ownership, target selection, or timeout behaviour.

   **Wrong behaviour:** The prose repeats nearby code and claims broader fidelity than the implementation provides. The timeout retention explanation specifically overlooks blocking finding 2.

   **Fix:** Replace the long module rationale with a short contract and RFC reference. Retain documentation of session scope, timeout, exception type, and ownership. Remove repeated caller history, call-site counts, and implementation narration. Fix timeout cleanup before deleting its justification.

   The inline comment audit proposes replacing or deleting 76 existing physical lines across these ranges. No deletions were applied. The timeout handling at `AttachedSessionClient.send` is the comment standard's `MUST KILL` structural finding; its justification cannot substitute for correct cleanup.

**Considered and cleared**

- **Event subscription inventory:** CDPRuntime registers `Page.frameAttached`, `Page.frameDetached`, `Page.frameNavigated`, `Runtime.executionContextCreated`, and `Runtime.executionContextDestroyed`. Screencast registers `Page.screencastFrame`. All callbacks are synchronous. The frame manager registers nothing itself. `curated` and `interstitial` add no subscriptions; their semantic waits use evaluation and polling.

- **Browser events and other targets:** None of those consumers subscribes to `Target.*`, enables target discovery, or attaches to child targets. I found no existing browser-session subscription that the adapter silently filters out. Neither runtime path establishes popup or out-of-process iframe sessions. CDP provides explicit attachment mechanisms for related targets. [Target protocol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ChromeDevTools/devtools-protocol/master/pdl/domains/Target.pdl) This clears the proposed missing-subscription finding, not full live parity. That requires a Chrome comparison with out-of-process iframe navigation and popup creation.

- **Explicit target ordering:** The old path reads `/json/list`, filters `type == "page"`, maps `id` to `targetId`, and sorts lexicographically. The new path reads `Target.getTargets`, applies the same page filter, and sorts `targetId`. Both use the same resolver for explicit numeric indexes and ID prefixes. Probes for `"1"`, `"2"`, and `"B"` agreed. The omitted-spec difference is blocking finding 1. Candidate-set parity for unusual hidden or prerender targets was not established.

- **Adapter attributes:** Current consumers use `connected`, `send`, `on`, `off`, and `disconnect`; all exist. Native snapshot and UID interaction receive the bound `send` method. No missing-attribute failure was found. Core `_connected` exists, so the private lookup works at this revision. It tracks the browser socket, however, and does not independently establish that the attached page remains alive.

- **Ordinary send exceptions:** Core catches ordinary exceptions from serialization and WebSocket sending and converts them to `ConnectionError`; the adapter translates that to the expected `CDPError`. This includes `TypeError`, `OSError`, and WebSocket closure errors. [WebSocket send contract](https://websockets.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/asyncio/client.html#websockets.asyncio.client.ClientConnection.send)

- **Cancellation fidelity:** Cancellation during WebSocket sending used to become `CDPError`; it now propagates `CancelledError`. Cancellation while waiting for a response already propagated in the old client. The probe confirmed that distinction. Preserving cancellation is defensible; cleanup must support it.

- **Timeout retention and correlation:** An unanswered cancelled request remains allocated until a response or connection cleanup. This is retention within the invocation, not a persistent cross-process leak. Request IDs increase monotonically, so late responses are not misrouted. The reader failure is blocking finding 2.

- **Normal teardown and partial initialization:** Normal shutdown marks the adapter closed, detaches the Target session, then closes the browser socket. Failures before the session yields unwind its own context. Ordinary failures after entry remain owned by the stack and are cleaned on normal stop. Browser death fails pending core requests. Suppressing expected detach/close errors after the operation has completed is reasonable; it does not hide the operation's own failure. Cancellation remains the exception above.

- **Deleted function and public export:** No source or test reference to `resolve_page_ws_url_async` remains. Production CLI paths no longer instantiate the page-level `CDPClient`. The package still publicly exports it, so it remains externally reachable. That export is not a runtime regression, and repository searches cannot establish that external consumers are absent.

- **RFC scope:** The attached-session requirement applies to CDPRuntime and its frame manager. This commit moves that foundation. The RFC's statement that it specifies no phasing does not itself prohibit an intermediate transport commit.

**Blocking**

1. **Omitting `--target` now fails when several pages exist.**

   **Location:** `src/browser_tools/cdp_handler.py:444`.

   **Trigger:** Run `bt INSTANCE frames list` with two page targets. A popup left open creates the same condition.

   **Wrong behaviour:** The old resolver selects the first page sorted by target ID when the spec is `None` (`cdp_client.py:280`). The new path passes `None` to `resolve_target`, which raises `AmbiguousTargetError` for several pages (`core/attach.py:127`). After the connection wait, the CLI reports that it could not open a CDP session.

   This affects more than commands where users can add `--target`. `frames`, `storage`, semantic waits, `detect`, and `screencast` do not expose that escape route.

   **Fix:** Preserve the handler's existing default by passing `"1"` with `"index"` when its target spec is absent. Keep the One-Shot Session's existing ambiguity policy for its other callers.

   **Evidence:** Resolver probes confirmed the old default selected `AAA`; the new default raised `AmbiguousTargetError`. A mocked-discovery `frames list` invocation returned exit 1 with empty stdout.

2. **A late response after timeout stops the reader and fails unrelated pending commands.**

   **Location:** `src/browser_tools/attached_session.py:114`; underlying delivery at `src/browser_tools/core/cdp_client.py:145`.

   **Trigger:** A CDP command exceeds its deadline, then Chrome returns its response while the invocation remains active. Cancellation of an outstanding screencast acknowledgement can create the same cancelled-future state.

   **Wrong behaviour:** `wait_for` cancels the core send and its awaited future. The core retains that future in `_pending`. When the response arrives, the reader calls `set_result` or `set_exception` on the cancelled future. This raises `InvalidStateError`, ends the receive loop, marks the connection disconnected, and fails other pending requests.

Python explicitly rejects setting a result on a completed or cancelled future. [Python Future contract](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-future.html#asyncio.Future.set_result)

   **Trigger:** The browser exits before discovery, the port is wrong, or the endpoint has no page targets.
