**Phase 2 merged** as `4676c5b`. Merged main verified: 1204 passing, one `main` branch.

**Phase 3 turned out to be two PRs, not one.** Reading the RFC's execution requirements against the code showed why: every verb opens its own connection, and a Step Run has to share one. That's a refactor touching both verb families, and bundling it with the new `run` verb would have made a PR where a behaviour change hides inside a large mechanical diff. So:

- **3a ([#129](https://github.com/dungle-scrubs/browser-tools/pull/129), CI running)** — make the session injectable. No new verb, no behaviour change; the suite stayed green across every step, which is the gate a pure refactor should have.
- **3b** — the engine: `run` verb, execution loop, failure semantics, `--timeout`, Run Document.

Two things worth calling out from 3a:

**It was smaller than I expected.** I'd budgeted 17 function splits. Three of the five One-Shot Session verbs were *already* split into "open session" and "work on session", so it came down to two extractions plus a helper. Phase 1 had also already done the hard part — converging `CDPHandler` onto the One-Shot Session means both families now sit on one transport, which is the only reason a single shared session is possible at all.

**One live result is the whole RFC in one line.** In the shared-session probe:

```

Over a shared session it isn't needed — the selection from an earlier operation is still in force. That property is working now, before the verb that will use it exists. The probe also confirms the session identity is unchanged end to end, so nothing quietly opened a second connection.

I deliberately did **not** give either family a second entry point. RFC-03 forbids that for the parser and preconditions, and the reason carries: one implementation can't drift from itself. An `X()` plus an `X_for_runs()` would be two things to keep in agreement forever.

Next: 3a review and merge, then 3b.

The agent talks plain. Not shorter, not clipped, not clever: plain. The

detail. When detail would bloat the answer, keep it behind a pointer to a
reference file or an explicit follow-up.

Rules:

1. Short sentences. One idea per sentence. Plain verbs, plain nouns,
   present tense where possible.

input.command:
git add src/browser_tools/cdp_handler.py tests/test_shared_session.py && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
fix(cdp): close a coroutine submit never scheduled

Self-review, prompted by writing the review brief for this PR.

`run_coroutine_threadsafe` takes ownership of a coroutine only when it
schedules it. `submit` has two paths where it does not: the runtime's loop
is None, and the loop is closed. Both raised and left the coroutine
untouched, so Python reported it at collection time:

    RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'body' was never awaited

In a Step Run that fires exactly when things are already going wrong. The
browser dies, the loop stops, and every remaining step's submit adds a
warning to the stderr the run is using to say which step failed.

The tell was in my own test: it called `coro.close()` after the expected
raise. A caller should not have to clean up after a function that refused
the work.

`submit` now closes the coroutine on every path where nothing took it, and
the test asserts both paths leave no warning behind rather than tidying up
itself.

Removing the close fails the new tests. 1222 passing.
EOF
git push 2>&1 | tail -2

## Behaviour preservation, proved live

The claim this PR rests on is that a verb called without `handler=` does
exactly what it did before. The green suite is evidence but not proof, so I ran
the nine-verb harness against real headless Chrome on `main` (`4676c5b`) and on
this branch, and diffed normalised transcripts.

Nineteen sections: navigate, snapshot, wait-idle, wait-stable, frames
list/select/reset, storage get with and without `--key`, detect, click, fill,
two fills from one snapshot (the v6 UID rule), a stale UID after navigation,
screencast, screenshot, and both target-resolution paths.

```
$ diff main.normalised branch.normalised
IDENTICAL
```

Byte for byte, once measured millisecond counts and per-run target IDs are
normalised. Both verb families are covered: the curated verbs that gained
`handler=`, and the One-Shot Session verbs whose bodies were extracted.

Transcripts are in `.scratch/rfc-03-phase3/`.

## One defect found while writing the review brief

`run_coroutine_threadsafe` takes ownership of a coroutine only when it
schedules it. `submit` had two paths where it does not: the runtime's loop is
`None`, and the loop is closed. Both raised and left the coroutine untouched:

```
RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'body' was never awaited
```

In a Step Run that fires at the worst moment. The browser dies, the loop stops,
and every remaining step's `submit` adds a warning to the same stderr the run is
using to report which step failed.

The tell was in my own test: it called `coro.close()` after the expected raise.
A caller should not have to clean up after a function that refused the work.
Fixed in `4703e7b`; `submit` now closes the coroutine on every path where
nothing took it, and the test asserts both paths leave no warning rather than
tidying up itself. Removing the close fails the new tests.

1222 passing.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
echo posted

Phase 3a is verified and waiting on the review.

**Phase 3a CI: all five green.** Merged-main comparison run live: **19 of 19 sections byte-identical** once per-run values are normalised. Both verb families covered. That's the direct proof the refactor preserves behaviour, which a green suite alone is not.

**One defect found, and the way I found it is the point.** Writing the adversarial brief for the reviewer made me list what could go wrong with `submit`. Item 3 on that list was "the coroutine never awaited when submit raises before scheduling". Then I checked my own code and it was true:

```
RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'body' was never awaited
```

`run_coroutine_threadsafe` only takes ownership when it schedules. Two paths don't — loop is `None`, loop is closed. In a Step Run that fires at the worst moment: the browser dies, the loop stops, and every remaining step's `submit` sprays a warning into the same stderr the run is using to report which step failed.

The tell was sitting in my own test. It called `coro.close()` after the expected raise. A test that cleans up after the code under test is describing a defect, not covering one. Fixed, and the test now asserts both paths leave no warning instead of tidying up itself.

That makes three separate occasions today where writing the *brief* — enumerating what an adversary would attack — found a bug before the adversary ran. Cheaper than the review itself.

The cross-family review is still running. When it returns I'll apply findings, merge, then build 3b: the `run` verb, execution loop, failure semantics, `--timeout`, and the Run Document.

Read-only session. I did not write `/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/.scratch/rfc-03-phase3/review-gpt6.md`. The report follows.

Reviewed `4703e7b827055d5c2e2d002bab9a301424c48bd7` against main at `4676c5beabb584bc04660f0f58ae1b3192aa17ad`. The branch advanced during review; this report includes the added coroutine-close fix.

**Blocking**

1. **A timed-out submission keeps running on the shared session.**  
   [cdp_handler.py:378](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/src/browser_tools/cdp_handler.py:378)

   Trigger: submit `capture_on_session(...)` with a deadline shorter than its blank-frame retry delay.

   Wrong behavior: `submit` raises `TimeoutError`, but the coroutine remains active. A probe recorded one `Page.captureScreenshot` at timeout and a second afterward. A separate probe against `4703e7b` confirmed that submitted work still produces effects after timeout.

   Phase 3b cannot safely treat that timeout as the end of the step. Work can overlap teardown or later use of the session. The caller receives neither the future nor another way to cancel that submission.

   Fix: retain the future, request cancellation when the blocking wait is interrupted or times out, and ensure task cleanup completes before the session is reused or closed. Track outstanding submissions through runtime shutdown. Cancellation cannot undo a command already sent.

**Non-blocking**

1. **`screenshot(handler=...)` ignores its handler.**  
   [curated.py:633](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/src/browser_tools/curated.py:633), [curated.py:644](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/src/browser_tools/curated.py:644)

   Trigger: call `screenshot(instance=None, handler=connected_handler)`.

   Wrong behavior: it resolves an Instance or External Endpoint and opens another One-Shot Session. It can fail despite having a usable supplied handler, or capture a separately selected target. A probe confirmed that port resolution still occurs.

   Fix: remove the unused parameter and require the Step Run to use `capture_on_session`, as the two-family design specifies. Alternatively, implement the parameter through `handler.session` and `handler.submit`. Do not silently accept it.

2. **`submit` accepts a stopped loop and can block its own loop thread.**  
   [cdp_handler.py:367](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/src/browser_tools/cdp_handler.py:367)

   Trigger: `_loop` exists but has stopped, including a shutdown race. Another trigger is calling `submit` from a coroutine or event callback on that loop.

   Wrong behavior: a stopped loop accepts the scheduling callback without executing it. A finite timeout expires; `timeout=None` can wait forever. A same-thread call blocks the thread needed to execute its coroutine. A finite-timeout probe produced `nested timed out`, followed by the child running afterward.

   Fix: reject same-loop calls. Coordinate submission and shutdown through runtime lifecycle state, and settle outstanding futures before closing the loop. An `is_running()` check alone cannot close the shutdown race.

   No production Step Run caller exists yet, so I could not establish a current CLI trigger. Python documents this submission API for use from another OS thread. [Python scheduling documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html#asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe)

3. **The raw pair loses command bounds and error translation.**  
   [attached_session.py:64](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/src/browser_tools/attached_session.py:64), [cdp_handler.py:353](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/src/browser_tools/cdp_handler.py:353)

   Trigger: Phase 3b submits a raw send or capture with no outer deadline, and Chrome leaves the command unanswered while keeping the connection open.

   Wrong behavior: the command has no deadline. A probe recorded `timeout=30.0` through the adapter and `timeout=None` through the raw capture helper. Raw calls also expose core `CDPError`, `ConnectionError`, and any explicit timeout directly. They bypass the adapter's closed-state check and automatic session attachment.

   This preserves the existing bare One-Shot Session behavior. It does not establish the RFC's claim that each step bounds itself. Calling the extracted helpers also bypasses the synchronous CLI error decorators.

   Fix: give the Step Run an explicit command-timeout policy and error boundary. Pass command bounds into core `send`, where pending requests are retired. Preserve deliberate unbounded waits. Map operational failures to exit 1 and usage failures to exit 2.

4. **Shared-session cleanup has existing gaps Phase 3b must handle.**  
   [events.py:344](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/src/browser_tools/events.py:344), [curated.py:558](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/src/browser_tools/curated.py:558)

   Trigger: `wait_on_session` registers a handler, then its domain-enable call raises `ConnectionError` or is cancelled. The cleanup `try/finally` begins after that await.

   Wrong behavior: the handler remains registered. A fake-client probe confirmed one remaining handler after enable failed. Separately, interrupting Bounded Capture during `_capture_for` skips `screencast_stop`; the supplied handler survives with its recorder still active.

   Fix: include domain enabling inside the wait's cleanup scope. Give Bounded Capture exception-safe operation cleanup without closing the borrowed handler. Phase 3b also needs the RFC's non-`Page`/`Runtime` domain-disable policy.

   These paths existed before this PR. Sharing the session makes their leftover state survive longer.

5. **The tests miss exception ownership and retry timing.**  
   [test_shared_session.py:85](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/tests/test_shared_session.py:85), [test_shared_session.py:164](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/tests/test_shared_session.py:164)

   Trigger: change `_handler_for` to stop a borrowed handler only when the body raises. Or remove the screenshot retry delay.

   Wrong behavior: the corresponding tests still pass. Both mutations were checked in memory. The ownership test exercises normal exit only. The retry test sets the delay to zero and asserts only the send count.

   Fix: raise inside the borrowed-handler context and then prove the handler remains usable. Replace sleep with a recording async stub and assert the delay between attempts, no delay after the final attempt, and the final returned data. Also assert target, registry, and `external` forwarding in the opener test.

6. **Two new docstring paragraphs repeat design justification.**  
   [curated.py:138](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/src/browser_tools/curated.py:138), [test_shared_session.py:14](/Users/kevin/dev/browser-tools/tests/test_shared_session.py:14)

   Trigger: a maintainer reads the ownership boundary or test module.

   Wrong behavior: both paragraphs argue that one implementation guarantees equivalent behavior. That claim exceeds what the interface and tests establish.

   Fix: delete these two paragraphs, eight nonblank prose lines. Retain the ownership contract, session-pair contract, and different-thread requirement. No `MUST KILL` suppression finding.

   Comment review ran inline using the installed `comment-sicko` rules. Independent review was unavailable because the model-routing command failed on npm network access.

**Considered and cleared**

- **Standalone behavior:** no modified verb changes target, endpoint, or registry handling when called without `handler=`. `snapshot`, `click`, and `fill` retain their target. `wait_idle`, `wait_stable`, `detect`, all three frame verbs, `storage_get`, and `screencast` now pass explicit `None`, equal to the opener's existing default. `_resolve_port` receives the same arguments. `external=endpoint is not None` reaches the opener.

- **Handler ownership:** `_handler_for` correctly leaves a supplied handler open after normal exit and body exceptions. An owned handler closes on normal exit, body exceptions, and explicit generator closure. These paths were probed. Production callers use `with`; no abandoned entered generator was found. No modified verb stops the supplied handler itself. Stopping Bounded Capture is a separate operation.

- **Raw-send extraction:** the four input prefixes and the `startswith(tuple)` test are unchanged. Hidden-tab refusal still precedes input delivery. The bare path still converts `HiddenTargetError` to `LifecycleError`. Focus refusal and `Target.createTarget` background normalization still run before the extracted helper. Phase 3b must preserve those outer checks.

- **Capture extraction:** its retry-loop AST is identical to main. Retry count, delay, blank detection, empty-data return, and final-attempt return are unchanged.

- **Scheduling failures:** commit `4703e7b` closes the coroutine when submission fails before scheduling. Its absent-loop and closed-loop tests pass. This fixes the leak found in the earlier commit.

- **Exception propagation and cancellation:** submitted exceptions retain their original traceback frames. Explicitly cancelling the returned asyncio bridge future reaches the coroutine's cleanup. The blocking finding is that `submit` does not request that cancellation on timeout.

- **Session availability:** production reads of `session` currently consist only of the handler's forwarding property. No unchecked production unpack exists. The pair can remain non-`None` after disconnect while `available` is false. Phase 3b must check readiness; the pair is not a liveness guarantee.

- **Concurrency and UID:** frame-manager operations and session event callbacks run on the runtime loop. Sequential successful submissions do not introduce a second frame-manager writer. UID resolution checks the live document token. No new stale-UID defect was established. Concurrent callers can still interleave multi-call verbs; Phase 3b's sequential execution must enforce ordering.

Validation: **58 focused tests passed** across shared-session, adapter, and One-Shot Session suites. Sources were loaded from the reviewed commit. An in-memory fixture kept profile roots isolated without filesystem writes. `git diff --check` passed. No live-browser or full Phase 3b integration test ran, so browser timing and final Run Document error handling remain unverified.

        cancelled = threading.Event()
        after_the_timeout: list[str] = []

        async def slow():
            started.set()
            try:

            except asyncio.CancelledError:

class TestAStepCleansUpAfterItselfOnTheSharedSession:
    """A leak that used to die with the process now outlives the step."""

    @pytest.mark.asyncio
    async def test_a_wait_unsubscribes_when_its_enable_fails(self):
        """`suppress(CDPError)` does not catch a dropped connection.

        The subscription is registered before the enable. If the enable
        raises anything but `CDPError`, the cleanup has to already be in
        scope, or the handler stays registered on a session later steps use
        and pushes into a queue nobody reads.
        """
        from browser_tools import events

        class Core:
            def __init__(self):
                self.handlers = {}

            def on(self, event, callback, session_id=None):
                self.handlers[event] = callback

            def off(self, event, callback):
                self.handlers.pop(event, None)

            async def send(self, **_kw):
                raise ConnectionError("socket gone")

        core = Core()
        with pytest.raises(ConnectionError):
            await events.wait_on_session(core, "S1", "Page.loadEventFired", None, 1)

fix(cdp): apply the cross-family review of the shared session

A gpt-6-astra review over Codex, implementer's family excluded. One blocking
finding, five non-blocking. It cleared behaviour preservation independently,
by comparing every modified verb against main.

**A timed-out submission kept running on the shared session.**

`submit` waited with `future.result(timeout)`. On a timeout the wait ended
and the coroutine did not: the reviewer's probe recorded one
`Page.captureScreenshot` at the deadline and a second one after it. Under a
Step Run that is work still going out over the session the next step is
about to use, and the one teardown is about to close. `submit` now cancels
the future, which reaches the coroutine and runs its cleanup. What was
already sent to the browser stays sent; this stops what has not happened
yet.

**`screenshot(handler=...)` accepted a handler and ignored it.**

My bulk signature edit added the parameter because the signature matched,
but `screenshot` runs over a One-Shot Session and never consults it. It
resolved an instance and opened a second session instead. A parameter that
is silently ignored is worse than an absent one, so it is gone; a Step Run
reaches this verb through `capture_on_session`.

**`submit` from the runtime's own loop would deadlock.** The loop would have
to run the coroutine and wait for it at the same time. Refused with a
message now.

**A wait could leave its subscription behind.** `wait_on_session` registers
the handler, then awaits the domain enable under `suppress(CDPError)`, which
does not catch `ConnectionError`. The `try/finally` that unsubscribes began
after that await. Outside a run the process ends and the leak with it; on a
shared session the handler stays registered and pushes into a queue nobody
reads. The cleanup scope now opens before the enable.

**Two tests passed against broken code.** The reviewer mutated
`_handler_for` to close a borrowed handler when the body raises, and removed
the screenshot retry delay; both suites stayed green. The first now raises
inside the borrowed context and asserts the session still works afterwards.
The second records the sleeps and asserts the delay, that there is none
after the final attempt, and that the final attempt's data is returned.

Also asserted target, registry and `external` forwarding in the opener test,
which was checking only the port.

Two docstring paragraphs claimed one implementation guarantees equivalent
behaviour. It does not: the session lifetime genuinely differs inside a run.
Rewritten to the ownership contract, which is what is true.

Not fixed here, recorded for Phase 3b: the raw `(client, sessionId)` pair
bypasses the adapter's 30s bound and its exception translation, so the
engine needs an explicit command-timeout policy and error boundary. Bounded
Capture interrupted mid-capture also skips `screencast_stop`.

Five mutations run, five caught, including both the reviewer's. 1228
passing. The live shared-session probe still passes end to end.

preservation independently, verb by verb against `main`, which matches the

|---|---|
| B1: a timed-out submission keeps running on the shared session | **Fixed** |
| N1: `screenshot(handler=...)` ignores its handler | **Fixed** by removing the parameter |
| N2: `submit` from the runtime's own loop deadlocks | **Fixed** |
| N3: the raw pair loses the 30s bound and error translation | **Recorded for 3b** |
| N4: a wait can leave its subscription registered | **Fixed** |
| N5: two tests pass against broken code | **Fixed** |
| N6: two docstring paragraphs overclaim | **Fixed** |

`submit` waited with `future.result(timeout)`. On a timeout the wait ends and
the coroutine does not. The reviewer's probe recorded one
`Page.captureScreenshot` at the deadline and a second one *after* it.

Under a Step Run that is work still going out over the session the next step is
about to use, and the one teardown is about to close. `--timeout` would have
stopped reporting and not stopped running.

`submit` now cancels the future, which reaches the coroutine and runs its
cleanup. What was already sent to the browser stays sent; this stops what has
not happened yet.

My bulk signature edit added `handler=` to `screenshot` because the signature
matched the others. `screenshot` runs over a One-Shot Session and never
consults it: it resolved an instance and opened a *second* session. A caller
passing a perfectly good handler would get a silent second connection, or a
failure while holding a usable one.

A parameter that is silently ignored is worse than an absent one. Removed. A
Step Run reaches this verb through `capture_on_session`.

`wait_on_session` registers its handler, then awaits the domain enable under
`suppress(CDPError)` - which does not catch `ConnectionError`. The
`try/finally` that unsubscribes began *after* that await.

Outside a run the process ends and the leak with it. On a shared session the
handler stays registered and keeps pushing into a queue nobody reads. The
cleanup scope now opens before the enable:

```

raises - exactly when a run must not lose its session - and both suites stayed
green. My test only exercised the clean exit. It now raises inside the borrowed
context and asserts the session still works afterwards.

The retry test set the delay to zero and counted sends, which a capture that
retried instantly would also pass. Instant retries are the thing the delay
exists to prevent: the page has not repainted, so every attempt returns the
same blank frame. It now records the sleeps and asserts the delay, that there
is none after the final attempt, and that the final attempt's data is returned.

Five mutations, five caught, including both of the reviewer's:

| Guard removed | Tests that fail |
|---|---|
| close a borrowed handler when the body raises | 1 |
| remove the screenshot retry delay | 1 |
| abandon a timed-out submission | 1 |
| allow submit from the runtime's own loop | 1 |
| narrow the wait's cleanup scope | 1 |

**1228 passing.** The live shared-session probe still passes end to end,
including `storage get` with no `--key` after a `frames select`.

### Carried to Phase 3b

- The raw `(client, sessionId)` pair bypasses `AttachedSessionClient`'s 30s
  command bound and its exception translation. The engine needs an explicit
  command-timeout policy and error boundary, mapping operational failures to
  exit 1 and usage failures to exit 2.
- Bounded Capture interrupted mid-capture skips `screencast_stop`, leaving the
  borrowed handler with its recorder active.
- The RFC's domain-disable policy for non-`Page`/`Runtime` domains.

# Turn `_print_json(X(...)); return EXIT_OK` into `return X(...)` inside the
# curated dispatch, so it yields the envelope rather than printing it.
start = s.index("def _run_curated(")
end = s.index("def _run_frames(")
block = s[start:end]

block = block.replace(
    "def _run_curated(args: argparse.Namespace, registry_path: str | None) -> int:",
    "def _curated_envelope(\n"
    "    args: argparse.Namespace,\n"
    "    registry_path: str | None,\n"
    "    handler: Any | None = None,\n"
    ") -> dict[str, Any]:",
)
block = re.sub(r"_print_json\(\n(\s+)(curated\.[a-z_]+\()", r"return \2", block)
block = block.replace("            )\n        )\n        return EXIT_OK\n", "        )\n")
block = block.replace("        return EXIT_OK\n\n    if args.command", "\n    if args.command")
block = block.replace(
    "    if args.command == \"frames\":\n        return _run_frames(args, registry_path)",
    "    if args.command == \"frames\":\n        return _frames_envelope(args, registry_path, handler)",
)
block = block.replace("    return EXIT_USAGE\n", "    raise PassthroughUsageError(f\"{args.command} is not a curated verb\")\n")
# Every curated call now forwards the session.
block = block.replace("                endpoint=args.endpoint,\n            )", "                endpoint=args.endpoint,\n                handler=handler,\n            )")
s = s[:start] + block + s[end:]
p.write_text(s)
print("converted")

git checkout -b feat/one-step-dispatch 2>&1|tail -1 && git status --porcelain && git add src/browser_tools/cli.py src/browser_tools/curated.py src/browser_tools/events.py src/browser_tools/list_verbs.py tests/test_step_dispatch.py && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
refactor(cli): one dispatch for every step-capable verb

RFC-03 Phase 3b, part one. A Step Run needs the JSON document a verb
produces, not the side effect of printing it, and it needs every verb to run
on the session the run already holds. This provides both through one
function. It adds no verb and changes no behaviour; the suite was green
across every step.

`cli.step_envelope(args, registry_path, handler)` returns what `_run` used
to print. `_run` now prints what it returns. A Step Run will collect it into
the Run Document instead, which is what makes a step's `result`
byte-identical to what the same step prints alone.

One dispatch, not two. A Step Run with its own table would be a second place
to add a verb and a second place to get it wrong. RFC-03 rules that out for
the parser and the preconditions, and the reason is the same here. A test
asserts the dispatch reaches every verb in `step_list.STEP_VERBS`, so a verb
that becomes a step without a branch fails the build rather than being
refused at runtime by a run that validation had already accepted.

To get there, `_run_curated` and `_run_frames` became `_curated_envelope`
and `_frames_envelope`, returning documents rather than printing and
returning exit codes.

**`screenshot` takes a `handler` again, and this time it uses it.** The
Phase 3a review found the parameter accepted and ignored, and offered two
fixes: remove it, or implement it through `handler.session` and
`handler.submit`. I removed it then because an ignored parameter is a trap.
This implements it, which is the half of that finding that was deferred.
`events.wait`, `list_verbs.console_list` and `list_verbs.network_list` get
the same treatment: given a handler they submit their `*_on_session`
coroutine to the run's loop; given none they open their own session exactly
as before.

Each submitted wait carries a bound derived from its own deadline, with
headroom, so the outer bound never fires first and turns a `WaitTimeout`
into something else. A `wait --timeout 0` submits with no bound, because 0
already means no deadline; the run's own `--timeout` is what bounds an
otherwise unbounded step.

Four mutations run, four caught: dropping the list verbs from the dispatch
fails 2 tests, dropping `wait` fails 1, dropping the curated family fails 5,
and forwarding `None` instead of the handler fails 3.

8 new tests, 1236 passing. The live shared-session probe still passes end to
end.

Part two is the engine: the `run` verb, the execution loop, failure
semantics, `--timeout`, and the Run Document.
EOF

gh pr create --title "refactor(cli): one dispatch for every step-capable verb" --body-file - <<'EOF'
RFC-03 Phase 3b, part one. A Step Run needs the JSON document a verb produces,
not the side effect of printing it, and it needs every verb to run on the
session the run already holds. This provides both through one function.

**No new verb and no behaviour change.** The suite was green across every step.
Part two is the engine.

## The seam

`cli.step_envelope(args, registry_path, handler)` returns what `_run` used to
print. `_run` now prints what it returns.

A Step Run will collect it into the Run Document instead. That is what makes a
step's `result` byte-identical to what the same step prints alone, which is the
composability RFC-03 specifies.

To get there, `_run_curated` and `_run_frames` became `_curated_envelope` and
`_frames_envelope`: they return documents rather than printing and returning
exit codes.

## One dispatch, and a guard that keeps it one

A Step Run with its own dispatch table would be a second place to add a verb
and a second place to get it wrong. RFC-03 rules that out for the parser and
the preconditions; the reason is identical here.

A test asserts the dispatch reaches every verb in `step_list.STEP_VERBS`. A
verb that becomes a step without a branch **fails the build**, rather than
being refused at runtime by a run that validation had already accepted. That is
the third guard of this shape in the RFC build, after the manual entry check and
the step-surface coverage check.

## `screenshot` takes a handler again, and uses it this time

The Phase 3a review found the parameter accepted and ignored, and named two
fixes: remove it, or implement it through `handler.session` and
`handler.submit`. I removed it then, because a silently ignored parameter is a
trap. This implements it, which is the half of that finding that was deferred.

`events.wait`, `list_verbs.console_list` and `list_verbs.network_list` get the
same treatment. Given a handler they submit their `*_on_session` coroutine to
the run's loop; given none they open their own session exactly as before.

Each submitted wait carries a bound derived from its own deadline, with
headroom, so the outer bound never fires first and turns a `WaitTimeout` into
something else. A `wait --timeout 0` submits with no bound, because `0` already
means no deadline there; the run's own `--timeout` is what bounds an otherwise
unbounded step.

## Verification

Four mutations, four caught:

| Guard removed | Tests that fail |
|---|---|
| the list verbs' branch | 2 |
| `wait`'s branch | 1 |
| the curated family's branch | 5 |
| forward `None` instead of the handler | 3 |

8 new tests, **1236 passing**. The live shared-session probe still passes end
to end, including `storage get` with no `--key` after a `frames select`.

## Next

Part two: the `run` verb, the execution loop, failure semantics, `--timeout`,
and the Run Document.

EOF

parts.text:
Phase 3a merged as `2f2a6ca`; Phase 3b split, and part one is open as [#130](https://github.com/dungle-scrubs/browser-tools/pull/130).

**What 3b-i does.** A Step Run needs the JSON document a verb produces, not the side effect of printing it, and every verb has to run on the session the run already holds. `cli.step_envelope` now returns what `_run` used to print, and `_run` prints what it returns. All thirteen step verbs go through it. No new verb, no behaviour change — 1236 passing, live probe still green.

**A guard that forces a decision, the third of this shape.** A test asserts the dispatch reaches every verb in `STEP_VERBS`. Add a verb to the step surface without a branch and the build fails, rather than a run refusing at runtime a step that validation had already accepted. The manual-entry check and the step-surface coverage check are the other two. That pattern has been the most reliable thing in this build: the failure lands on whoever adds the verb, not on a user months later.

**I reversed one Phase 3a decision, deliberately.** That review found `screenshot(handler=...)` accepted and ignored, and offered two fixes: remove the parameter, or implement it. I removed it then, because a silently ignored parameter is a trap and 3a was a refactor. This implements it — the half of the finding that was deferred, not a change of mind. `events.wait` and both list verbs got the same treatment.

**Why 3b split.** Same reason 3a did. The dispatch change is mechanical and behaviour-preserving, so a green suite is a real gate for it. The engine is new behaviour, where a green suite proves much less. Putting them in one PR would hide the second inside the first.

Four mutations this round, four caught. I picked them against the guarantees rather than the lines, as I said I would: drop a family from the dispatch, forward `None` instead of the handler.

Next: 3b-ii — the `run` verb, execution loop, failure semantics, `--timeout`, and the Run Document.

2

4	`_run` prints what it returns; a Step Run will collect it into the Run
5	Document instead. That is what makes a step's `result` byte-identical to what
6	the same step prints alone, which is the composability RFC-03 specifies.
7

9	and a second place to get it wrong. RFC-03 rules that out for the parser and
10	for the preconditions, and the reason is the same here.
11	"""

26	        self.stopped = False
27	        self.seen: list[str] = []
28	        self.session = ("CLIENT", "SESSION-1")
29	        self.available = True
30	        self.connect_error = None
31

33	        from browser_tools.lifecycle import LifecycleError
34

37	        return self.session

40	        self.stopped = True
41	
42	    def call_native(self, name, arguments):

44

CI caught a defect I'd have shipped: **Lint & Type Check failed** on #130. Tests passed — pyright didn't.

```
curated.py:648 - error: "None" is not iterable
```

`CDPHandler.session` is `tuple[Any, str] | None` and I unpacked it in four places without checking. The Phase 3a reviewer had already described this exact shape, in its *cleared* list: the pair is `None` before the connection comes up, and it survives a disconnect while `available` is false, so it is not a liveness guarantee. I read that, agreed with it, recorded it as carried to 3b — and then wrote the unchecked unpack anyway.

Unpacked blind, both cases become `TypeError: cannot unpack non-sequence NoneType` at the point of use. Inside a Step Run that would be the diagnostic a user gets when the browser dies mid-run.

`CDPHandler.require_session()` now returns the pair or raises `LifecycleError` carrying the runtime's own `connect_error` — the reason the connection failed, not a Python type complaint. A cast would have silenced pyright and kept the bad failure mode; the type error was pointing at a real one.

**My local gate was wrong.** I had been running `ruff check` and the suite and calling that clean. CI runs `ruff check` *and* `pyright src/`. Pyright is now in my local pass, and it is clean along with 1240 tests and the live probe.

Waiting on the re-run, then review and merge #130, then 3b-ii: the `run` verb, execution loop, failure semantics, `--timeout`, Run Document.

parts.text:
Switched to a new branch 'feat/run-verb'
### The Manual entry (normative)

`tests/test_guide.py` enumerates verbs from the parser and fails the build when one
has no entry, so `run` cannot ship without this. The following is the normative
text. It belongs in `GUIDE.txt` after the CURATED VERBS block, as its own section.

```
RUNNING MANY STEPS IN ONE INVOCATION

  run FILE [--timeout SECONDS]
  run -    [--timeout SECONDS]
      Run an ordered list of steps against one browser, in one invocation, over
      one CDP connection. FILE is the list; `-` reads it from stdin. Takes
      [INSTANCE] and --endpoint URL as above, and --target SPEC or --url
      SUBSTRING to pick the page the whole run drives.

      One step per line, each line a verb phrase exactly as you would type it
      after the instance name. Blank lines and lines starting with # are
      ignored. Lines are split the way a shell splits them, so quoting works as
      it does at the prompt.

          # select the checkout frame once, then read it twice
          frames select checkout
          storage get
          Page.getNavigationHistory '{}'
          snapshot

      This is not a scripting language. There are no variables, no conditions,
      no loops, and no way for one step to use another step's output. A run does
      what the same commands would do one after another; it cannot decide
      anything. Where you need a decision, read the output and run again.

      A STEP IS A VERB, NOT AN INVOCATION. Steps may be: snapshot, click, fill,
      wait-idle, wait-stable, wait, detect, console-list, network-list, frames,
      storage get, screenshot, screencast, and any raw Domain.method. A step may
      NOT name an instance, --endpoint, --target or --url: those belong to the
      run, which resolves them once. attach is not a step (it runs until stdin
      ends, so nothing could follow it), and neither are launch, status, stop,
      cleanup, profile, window-border, guide or help. Any of these in a step
      list is a usage error (exit 2).

      FRAME SELECTION LASTS. `frames select` in one step governs the steps after
      it, so `storage get` with no --key works inside a run. A selection
      remembers the pattern you gave it, so after a navigation it re-points at
      whatever frame now matches. If nothing matches any more, the selection is
      cleared and the next frame-scoped step fails rather than reading the wrong
      frame. The selected frame going away clears it too, but the pattern is
      kept either way, so a later navigation that brings a matching frame back
      selects it again. Only `frames reset` and a new `frames select` change the
      pattern.

      EVERYTHING ELSE BEHAVES AS IT WOULD ALONE, WITH ONE EXCEPTION. A step
      inside a run does what the same command does on its own. Domains a step
      turns on are turned off when that step ends, so a second `network-list`
      in one run sees what the first one saw.

  run FILE [--timeout SECONDS]
  run -    [--timeout SECONDS]
      Run an ordered list of steps against one browser, in one invocation, over
      one CDP connection. FILE is the list; `-` reads it from stdin. Takes
      [INSTANCE] and --endpoint URL as above, and --target SPEC or --url
      SUBSTRING to pick the page the whole run drives.

      One step per line, each line a verb phrase exactly as you would type it
      after the instance name. Blank lines and lines starting with # are
      ignored. Lines are split the way a shell splits them, so quoting works as
      it does at the prompt.

          # select the checkout frame once, then read it twice
          frames select checkout
          storage get
          Page.getNavigationHistory '{}'
          snapshot

      This is not a scripting language. There are no variables, no conditions,
      no loops, and no way for one step to use another step's output. A run does
      what the same commands would do one after another; it cannot decide
      anything. Where you need a decision, read the output and run again.

      A STEP IS A VERB, NOT AN INVOCATION. Steps may be: snapshot, click, fill,
      wait-idle, wait-stable, wait, detect, console-list, network-list, frames,
      storage get, screenshot, screencast, and any raw Domain.method. A step may
      NOT name an instance, --endpoint, --target or --url: those belong to the
      run, which resolves them once. attach is not a step (it runs until stdin
      ends, so nothing could follow it), and neither are launch, status, stop,
      cleanup, profile, window-border, guide or help. Any of these in a step
      list is a usage error (exit 2).

      FRAME SELECTION LASTS. `frames select` in one step governs the steps after
      it, so `storage get` with no --key works inside a run. A selection
      remembers the pattern you gave it, so after a navigation it re-points at
      whatever frame now matches. If nothing matches any more, the selection is
      cleared and the next frame-scoped step fails rather than reading the wrong
      frame. The selected frame going away clears it too, but the pattern is
      kept either way, so a later navigation that brings a matching frame back
      selects it again. Only `frames reset` and a new `frames select` change the
      pattern.

      EVERYTHING ELSE BEHAVES AS IT WOULD ALONE, WITH ONE EXCEPTION. A step
      inside a run does what the same command does on its own. Domains a step
      turns on are turned off when that step ends, so a second `network-list`
      in one run sees what the first one saw.

parts.text:
The exception is the Page and Runtime domains. A run needs them on
      throughout to track frames, so they are never turned off between steps.
      A step that relies on being the first to turn one of them on does not
      get that. `wait --event Runtime.executionContextCreated` after any step
      that touched Runtime reports nothing, where the same command on its own
      reports the contexts that already exist; `console-list` is in the same
      position, because it turns Runtime on too. Run either one on its own.

      A raw step you write yourself is yours to undo. `raw Network.enable {}`
      stays on until a later step turns it off; the rule above covers only the
      domains a verb turns on for you.

      UIDS ARE UNCHANGED. A UID is still valid until the page navigates, no
      longer and no shorter. One process does not extend it. Because no step can
      read another step's output, every UID in a step list is one you put there
      from a snapshot you already read.

      IT STOPS AT THE FIRST FAILURE, and nothing rolls back. A step that has run
      has already reached the browser. Steps after the failure do not run.

      --timeout SECONDS bounds the whole run; without it there is no whole-run
      deadline, because every step already bounds itself. Use it when a step
      opts out of its own bound, as `wait --timeout 0` does.

      OUTPUT. One JSON document, on success and on failure alike: a `run` object
      with the step count, how many completed, and the status; and a `steps`
      array with one entry per step attempted, each carrying the JSON that step
      would have printed alone. Steps never reached are absent.

      READ IT IN THIS ORDER: the exit code, then `run.status`, then the steps.
      A failed run still contains successful step entries, and each of those
      carries exactly what that step prints on its own. If you parse the steps
      without checking the exit code first, a run that died at step 7 reads
      like a run that finished.

      Exit 0   every step succeeded.
      Exit 1   a step failed, or the run timed out. The document is still
               printed, so you can see what already ran. This is the one verb
               that prints on stdout when it exits 1.
      Exit 2   the step list was malformed, or a step named an instance,
               --endpoint, --target or --url. The whole list is checked before
               the first step runs, so nothing ran.
```

The OUTPUT AND EXIT CODES block at `GUIDE.txt:333-346` also changes, so a caller
reading only that block learns about the exception. Its Exit 1 line becomes:

```
  Exit 1   operational failure: the browser is gone, a CDP call failed, a
           deadline passed, a profile is held, a UID no longer resolves.
           Nothing is printed on stdout, except by `run`, which prints its
           run document so you can see which steps already ran.
```

@~/.agents/GLOBAL.md

# Claude Code Instructions

These instructions apply only to Claude Code, layered on the global
instructions imported above.

## Model selection and delegation

Two skills own this; nothing here restates them.

- `choose-model` picks the route (model through harness) from its
  registry. Same query, same answer. Query it before any delegation where
  the model is not pinned by the user or by the calling skill's own spec.

  Every `Agent` spawn, every `Workflow` `agent()` call, and every agent
  started in a terminal you control is a delegation. The last one includes
  `herdr agent start` and any successor session you launch to carry on work.
  This includes spawns you would describe as fanning out your own reading,
  searching, or exploring. There is no unrouted subagent. A pane is not an
  exemption: `--kind claude` selects a harness, not a model, so a launch with
  no model argument inherits whatever that harness defaults to. A spawn that
  carries no explicit `model:` inherits the session model, which the
  registry ranks last for most task types - so an unrouted fan-out is not
  neutral, it is the worst route chosen by accident.

  The query is its own tool block and precedes the block that spawns.
  Never send the query and the spawn together. Bundling independent calls
  is right in general and wrong here: the spawn depends on the query.
- `delegate` runs the pick: your subagent tool for a same-harness route,
  `scripts/delegate.ts` over `hcn run` for every other route, walking the
  fallbacks on hcn's typed failure classes and reporting which route
  actually produced the result. Never a raw `codex exec`, `pi -p`, or
  `muse exec`.

Cross-family reviewers: query with `excludeFamilies` set to the
implementer's family. Never silently run an adversarial role on the same
family as the majority; if cross-family was unavailable, say so in the
synthesis.

Claude Code mechanics, which the skills cannot carry because they are
harness-neutral:

- **Same-harness routes** (`harness: claude`) run through the `Agent` or
  `Workflow` `model:` parameter with the route's `modelId` and `effort`.
  Pass the model explicitly on every spawn: subagents inherit the session
  model when `model:` is omitted, so omitting it silently routes the work
  to whatever the session happens to be running. Label the spawn with the
  route. Tool scope there comes from the agent
  type, not the call: `delegate.ts --plan` shows the access the task
  defaults to; `read` means a read-only agent type (Explore, or a project
  agent defined with read tools), `write` means general-purpose.
- **Every other route runs through a wrapper.** The `model:` parameter
  takes Claude models only, so a non-Claude route inside a Workflow stage
  or a background Agent is a `model:'sonnet'`, `effort:'low'` wrapper
  whose whole job is: write the brief to a file, run
  `npx tsx ~/.agents/skills/delegate/scripts/delegate.ts --choice <choice.json> --brief <brief.md> --out <report.json>`
  via Bash, and return the report. Use `schema` on the wrapper when
  structured output is needed. **Label the wrapper with the route**,
  e.g. `{label:'glm-5.3@pi:impl'}`, `{label:'gpt-5.6-sol@codex:review-auth'}`:
  the UI shows the wrapper's Claude model, and the label is the only
  visible record of the real worker. When the walk advanced, the
  report's `actual` names the route that did the work; carry that into
  whatever the stage reports.
- **A terminal-launched session takes its route on the command line.** The
  chosen `modelId` and `effort` reach the launch arguments, the same as a
  `model:` parameter would. When the harness cannot express the route, say so
  and name the route you asked for; do not launch unrouted and report the
  model afterwards.
- A single delegation from the main session needs no wrapper: run
  `delegate.ts` from Bash directly. The wrapper exists to keep a
  long-running hcn turn and its events out of the session's context.
- hcn turns can exceed Bash's 10-minute default timeout. Pass an explicit
  Bash timeout or background the run and poll the `--out` report file.
- Parallel implementation stages that edit code use `isolation:'worktree'`
  so off-Claude edits do not collide in the shared checkout.
- Workflow token budgets count Claude tokens only. Off-Claude work is
  invisible to `budget.spent()` but metered on its own provider;
  invisibility is not a license to fan out.

Routing by pipeline shape:

- Off-Claude implementation stages belong where the work is parallel and
  isolatable. In a sequential pipeline whose stages build on one
  uncommitted working tree, keep implementation on in-process Claude
  agents; a worktree-isolated off-Claude stage would need a merge step
  between every stage. Accepted trade, not a rubric violation.
- Read-only off-Claude stages (review, investigation, analysis) fit any
  pipeline shape.
- Verification gates that only run lint, typecheck, and tests and fix
  trivial breakage: `sonnet` at low effort. A gate that must judge
  ambiguous failures (pre-existing vs regression, fix the test vs fix the
  code): `opus`, escalating to `fable` only when the call is genuinely
  hard.
- Small clear-spec cleanups route off Claude like everything else. The
  only work kept inline on a Claude agent is a single-edit change cheaper
  to make than to describe.

## Shell and worktrees

- **Capture an exit status before you filter output.** `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is
  Bash; under zsh it reads empty and reports nothing. Use zsh's `pipestatus`,
  or capture `$?` on its own line before any pipe. A command whose output you
  pipe into `grep`, `head` or `tail` reports the filter's status, not its own.
  Make every dependent step conditional on the real status: a build chained
  after a failed check with `;` runs anyway, and its success reads as though
  the check passed.
- **The Bash tool evaluates with zsh semantics.** An unquoted `$var` does not
  word-split, and an unmatched glob is a hard error rather than a literal.
  Pass multi-word argv through a function using `"$@"` or an array, and quote
  arguments carrying globs. A loop feeding `cmd $arg` turns every multi-word
  case into one argument with spaces inside, so every case can report the same
  wrong answer.
- **A separate worktree over a dirty tree is built, not entered.**
  `EnterWorktree` and `git worktree add` start from HEAD and carry none of the
  uncommitted work. When the task must build on a dirty tree and stash, revert
  and commit are forbidden: create the worktree from HEAD; apply
  `git diff HEAD --binary` from the main checkout inside it; rsync the
  untracked files, excluding caches; add the worktree directory to the main
  checkout's `.git/info/exclude`. Verify the transfer by diffing the two
  sorted porcelain status lists, each captured in its own command, before
  entering.
- **Under `EnterWorktree` isolation the Bash tool refuses commands it cannot
  verify stay inside the worktree**: git combined with subshells or process
  substitution, heredoc-written programs, and programs computed at runtime.
  Write the command to a file with the Write tool and run it plainly
  (`bash <file>`, `python3 <file>`). After the first refusal, put complex
  verification and comparison steps in script files from the start.

# Global Agent Instructions

These instructions apply across local repositories and tools on this machine.

## General Guidelines

- Never use em dashes. Use plain dash "-" instead.
- When writing commit messages, NEVER auto-add your agent name as co-author.
- Never manually modify CHANGELOG.md files or any files marked as
  auto-generated.
- When making technical decisions, give development cost little weight.
  Prefer quality, simplicity, robustness, scalability, and long term
  maintainability.
- When scaffolding a project, always ask the user whether to use XDG
  standards when applicable. Wait for their answer before choosing the
  affected directory layout or file locations.
- When fixing a bug, first reproduce it end-to-end, as close as possible to
  how an end user hits it. This finds the real problem, so the fix solves
  it.
- When configuring, integrating, or debugging a third-party tool, library,
  or framework, consult its current official documentation before
  reverse-engineering behavior from error messages. Reach for the docs the
  moment you are guessing at version-specific behavior or at how two tools
  interact, or after two attempts have not converged.
- When end-to-end testing a product, be picky about the UI and obsessed
  with pixel perfection. If something clearly looks off, even outside the
  current task, try to get it fixed.
- Apply the same standard to lint, test failures, and test flakiness: fix
  them even when the current work did not cause them.

## Fit Check

A possibility is not a mandate. That a capability can be built, that a
reviewer says it is missing, or that a planning session surfaced it does
not mean it belongs in the product. Before any functionality decision (what
the product does for its users is about to be added, removed, or changed),
run the fit check. Reorganization (refactor, cleanup, lint) is outside it.

- Who uses this? Name the actual users and what they do with it.
- What is the product for? One sentence, from `CONTEXT.md`, the README,
  or the request. If none states it, ask before building.
- Does the candidate serve that purpose? No: decline it and record why.
  Unclear: it is the user's decision, with a recommended answer.
- What does it cost to keep? Name the upkeep it adds after it ships and
  weigh it against that use. Build cost gets little weight; upkeep is paid
  for as long as the capability exists. Upkeep larger than the use:
  decline it, even though it fits.
- Which way does it move the scope? Widen, hold, or narrow. Name the
  direction; widen and narrow are the user's call. Narrow is a valid
  answer.

The full ruleset, the moments it fires, and the record a declined
candidate leaves are the `fit-check` skill.

## Task Artifacts

A harness scratchpad or temp directory does not survive the session. Files
there can be gone by the next session, including one that resumes the same
work. Keep throwaway output there, and nothing else.

A task's decision ledger, its evidence (scripts, captures, measurements),
any git worktree or working checkout the task created, any branch not yet
merged, and any report a later reader must reach go in a durable place
instead.
Default to `.scratch/<task>/` inside the repository the work belongs to,
git-ignored. It sits beside the code it is about, `git status` keeps it
visible, and cleanup is one directory removal in one place. Use
`~/.agents/tasks/<task>/` only when the work has no single home repository
or spans several. Name that path in the task's checkpoint and in the final
report, so the record is findable after the session ends.

A linked worktree stores absolute paths, in its own `.git` file and in the
parent's `.git/worktrees/<name>/gitdir`. Renaming or moving either side
breaks git commands inside that worktree while leaving its trees and commits
intact. Repair it from the main checkout with
`git worktree repair <path>...`, naming every moved worktree; it rewrites
the links and nothing else.

Evidence that a committed file cites is not task scratch. A comment or a
document that points at a git-ignored path resolves on one machine and
nowhere else. Commit that evidence into the repository, or cite the
finding rather than the path.

## Repository Instruction Files

- `AGENTS.md` is the canonical instruction file at every repository scope;
  all harness-independent guidance goes there.
- Every directory with an `AGENTS.md` has a sibling `CLAUDE.md` whose first
  non-comment instruction imports `@AGENTS.md`. Below the import: Claude
  Code-specific mechanics only, never duplicated shared guidance.
- Local, untracked guidance follows the same pattern: `AGENTS.local.md`
  for harness-independent local instructions, `CLAUDE.local.md` importing
  it. Both are git-ignored; `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` stay trackable.
  Never use `AGENTS.override.md` for additive local guidance - Codex
  treats it as a replacement for the sibling `AGENTS.md`.
- Apply scopes from the repository root toward the working directory. At
  each level apply tracked guidance first, then that scope's
  `AGENTS.local.md` when it exists and is not already in context. Skip
  local files from scopes that do not govern the current work.

## Identity and Publishing

- The GitHub scope is `dungle-scrubs`; the `gh` CLI authenticates as that
  user. Publish under the matching scope, e.g. `@dungle-scrubs/<name>`.
  Never guess a package name or scope - this is it.
- Never distribute my open source projects through Homebrew: no formula,
  no cask, no `brew install` line in their install instructions. Prefer
  npm for anything Node/Bun-adjacent, else a direct install script.
  Installing other people's tools with Homebrew stays fine.

## Important Local Repositories

Under `~/dev`; useful context for agent sessions.

- `~/dev/launchdawg` - reconciler for macOS user LaunchAgents
  (`~/.config/launchdawg/services.yml`).
- `~/dev/opchain` - CLI for 1Password service-account workflows.
- `~/dev/ansible` - source of truth for the macOS Kanata unit. Before
  Kanata setup or recovery, install its skill with the repository's
  `kanata_skill` Ansible tag and start a new agent session.
- `~/dev/skills` - source of truth for the shared skill library, deployed
  to `~/.agents/skills` by its link script. `~/dev/skills-old` is
  abandoned; do not work in it, and nothing deploys from it.

## References

Load on the trigger, not otherwise.

| When a task involves | Read |
|---|---|
| Host selection, remote access, machine capabilities, keeping dev machines synchronized | `~/.agents/references/home-network.md` |
| Running a model on a local endpoint, or picking the local model or machine for some work | `~/.agents/references/local-inference.md` |
| Agent hooks, agent config files, or a tool that wants to install itself into an agent | `~/.agents/references/agents-setup.md` |

## Local Ports

Before starting, configuring, or changing a local development server, read
`~/.agents/PORTS.md`. Use the assigned port when the service is listed;
give a new long-running service an unused port from the reserved range and
add its row so the registry stays the source of truth. Bind every local
server to loopback (`127.0.0.1`), never to all interfaces; a wider bind
needs the user's explicit request, scoped to that one server.

## Private Data and Local Inference

The privacy override: work that would put secret material into a hosted
model's context runs on a local model instead. Secret material: environment
variables and `.env` files, API tokens, credentials, private keys,
`1Password` output, terminal output from a production host, and anything
the user calls private. Hosted models are disqualified, including
whichever agent is reading this. Privacy work never reroutes to a hosted
model, even when no local model is reachable: say the work cannot be done
on this machine instead.

Credential and key fields inside local tool stores are secret material too,
for example a Cursor chat store's `blobEncryptionKey`. Explore such a store
by printing structure only: field names, shapes, lengths, counts. Never
select or decode the credential value in a hosted session; tool output
enters the model's context when it prints. If the value itself must be
read, run that read on a local model with a pointer to the file.

A gate denial is answered by the route the denial names, never by reshaping
the input until the gate stops matching. Renaming a credential file, moving
it, or splitting the command so the pattern no longer fires leaves the same
value flowing into the same hosted context, with the record now showing a
pass. If the denial looks wrong, say so and leave it in place; a gate whose
false positives get worked around is a gate that protects nothing.

Run it as a separate process, through the `delegate` skill with a
`choose-model` query carrying `privacy: secret`: the only eligible routes
are local, and the walk adds the containment flags itself. Compose the
prompt with pointers, not payloads - file paths, command names, line
numbers - and let the local model read the secret material on-machine. A
prompt that quotes the token has already leaked it, whichever model
answers.

The by-hand hcn run, the containment flags and why each one matters, the
air port forward, and the Herdr pane recipe are in
`~/.agents/references/local-inference.md` under "Private data".

## Codex

These are Codex-only mechanics. They live here because `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`
is a symlink to this file and Codex has no import directive.

`apply_patch` takes one file and one operation per call. A path carries a
single operation, so a rewrite is one `*** Update File` hunk, never
`*** Delete File` followed by `*** Add File`. Every `@@` needs at least one
`+` or `-` line under it: a context-only hunk, or a bare `@@`, swallows the
next `*** Update File:` header and fails the whole call. The call is atomic,
so one stale hunk in the fourth file discards the first three, and the error
names only the file that failed, which is usually not the one at the top of
the patch. Send one file per envelope.

`exec_command` owns every process it starts, and kills it when that call
returns. A daemon started inside one call is gone by the next: the launcher
reports a PID and exits 0, then the process is not running and nothing can
attach to it. Keep a long-lived process alive one of two ways: hold the exec
session open and drive it with `write_stdin` against its `session_id`, or
start it in a Herdr pane. Relaunching is not the fix; the second launch dies

The command guard scans the entire script string, so a single `rm -f` or
`rm -rf` anywhere rejects the whole `exec_command` call, including every
unrelated command bundled with it. Delete with `/usr/bin/trash`, and never
bundle a delete with work you cannot afford to lose.

## Tool Proxy

If the tool-proxy MCP is available, call `discover_tools` with a
plain-language description of the task before using any CLI or raw API for
an external service. Do not guess tool names; discovery expands from there.

Algolia, GA4, GCS, Google Search Console, GTM, Intercom,
Laravel Cloud, Namecheap, Notion, Rack Warehouse, Postgres, Reviewsion,
Sentry, Shopify, Vultr, WorkOS.

Two CLIs cover this. They are not interchangeable. Pick by task.

`chrome-devtools-axi` is the default. It drives a page: `open`, `snapshot`,
`click`, `fill`, `screenshot`, and a multi-step flow through `run`. It is the
only one with performance tooling: `lighthouse`, `perf-start` / `perf-stop` /

geolocation. `CHROME_DEVTOOLS_AXI_AUTO_CONNECT=1` attaches to the running
Chrome, so a logged-in session needs no profile copy.

task when it needs any of these:

- an event stream, or a blocking wait on one event (`attach`, `wait`),
- a named persistent profile, or several browsers at once,

  window in the background. `chrome-devtools-axi` guarantees neither.

automation tools. That sentence is the tool's own description of itself. This
section supersedes it.

session start and prints the repository, open issues, and open PRs. Add
`--json` for output an agent parses. `gh api` reaches anything the
subcommands miss.

Never manage, validate, or comment on the user's emotions. You are not a
person, and the user does not want your read on how they feel.

When the user asks a question while a task runs, answer it in the next
message, then continue the task. Never hold the answer for the end-of-turn
summary. If the answer depends on work not yet done, say so and say when
the answer will come.

Report a privacy incident in the message where it happens. A credential
printed into a hosted session, a secret file read in full, or private data
sent outward is named immediately with what to rotate, then the task
continues. Never hold it for the end-of-turn summary.

State a cause only when the evidence establishes it. An explanation
already in hand is not evidence for the case in front of you: check the
current one before reaching for it. Say which stage is confirmed and which
is not. Absent records establish nothing - an empty log is not proof that a
thing failed, nor that it succeeded. Never call partial evidence
confirmation; "the logs confirm it" over a zero-byte file is a claim about
the file, not about the event.

set of findings - open it with `open "<absolute path>"` before you present

app for that file type, so name no editor. A file meant for browser viewing
goes through the `open-in-browser` skill instead. A file written for an
agent or a tool to consume stays closed. When the opener fails, say the file
did not open.

stale process and start the right one.

|                                            |
|  Canvas frame "N2 Gapped Index"            |
|  Bring Pen to the front                    |
+--------------------------------------------+

in `~/.agents/skills/talk-normal/references/BANNED.md`, enforced by the

  project's `CONTEXT.md` or its canonical term, no analogies or metaphor.

subcommands miss.

## Communication

Never manage, validate, or comment on the user's emotions. You are not a
person, and the user does not want your read on how they feel.

When the user asks a question while a task runs, answer it in the next
message, then continue the task. Never hold the answer for the end-of-turn
summary. If the answer depends on work not yet done, say so and say when
the answer will come.

Report a privacy incident in the message where it happens. A credential
printed into a hosted session, a secret file read in full, or private data
sent outward is named immediately with what to rotate, then the task
continues. Never hold it for the end-of-turn summary.

State a cause only when the evidence establishes it. An explanation
already in hand is not evidence for the case in front of you: check the
current one before reaching for it. Say which stage is confirmed and which
is not. Absent records establish nothing - an empty log is not proof that a
thing failed, nor that it succeeded. Never call partial evidence
confirmation; "the logs confirm it" over a zero-byte file is a claim about
the file, not about the event.

When you write a file for the user to read - a report, a plan, a draft, a
set of findings - open it with `open "<absolute path>"` before you present
it, and keep the path in the reply. The system opener picks the user's own
app for that file type, so name no editor. A file meant for browser viewing
goes through the `open-in-browser` skill instead. A file written for an
agent or a tool to consume stays closed. When the opener fails, say the file
did not open.

When a command needs to run, run it yourself. Hand a command to the user
only when the agent genuinely cannot run it: interactive authentication
(`gcloud auth login`), commands that must outlive the session with no
service manager available, or actions the user must perform under their
own identity. "It is the user's dev server" is not a reason - kill the
stale process and start the right one.

A command that cannot run in the agent's own shell but does not need
`sudo` still runs without the user when Herdr is available (the `herdr`
skill is installed and `HERDR_ENV=1`). Create a new Herdr pane, run the
command there, read the pane to confirm the command succeeded, then close
the pane. This rule is the user's explicit request to use Herdr for that
case. The agent reads the pane output, so the command must not print
secret material; redirect it to a file instead. A command that a hook or
permission gate denied does not go to a pane: the denial is deliberate,
and a pane run goes around it. Hand the command to the user only when it
needs `sudo`, when a gate denied it, when Herdr is not available, or when
the pane run fails.

Ticket succession is authorized the same way. A session working a map,
having recorded its resolution, may start its successor in a Herdr pane and
close its own pane, without asking each time. This rule is the user's
explicit request for that case. It covers only the successor's pane and the
finishing session's own pane; every other pane lifecycle action still needs
its own approval. The finishing session closes itself only when the handoff
is complete and its final message carries nothing recorded nowhere else.

When handing over a command (only in those cases): print the complete
command, copy it to the clipboard with `pbcopy`, and frame it in an ASCII
`+`/`-`/`|` border with `COPIED TO CLIPBOARD` inside the top edge, one
blank bordered line above the command, sized so the command fits on one
line untruncated.

When the user's attention needs to move to a different surface - a served
page, an app window, a canvas, a file - say so before continuing. Open it
when you can. When you cannot bring it into view, print an ASCII box:

```
+--------------------------------------------+
| LOOK HERE - PEN.APP                        |
|                                            |
|  Canvas frame "N2 Gapped Index"            |
|  Bring Pen to the front                    |
+--------------------------------------------+
```

Name the surface, the address or location, and what to do there. Keep an
address stable once given; do not move a served page to a new port. Work
split across two surfaces without naming which one is live leaves the user
guessing, and a moving address makes "look at the page" unusable even when
you do say it.

Voice rules, always on. The named phrasings behind each rule are patterns
in `~/.agents/skills/talk-normal/references/BANNED.md`, enforced by the
phrase gate; the full register is the talk-normal skill.

- Never acknowledge, name, or validate an emotional state, and never
  apologize for the user's feelings. Acknowledge a factual mistake
  plainly and move on.
- No reassurance, empathy statements, or tone-policing; respond to the
  substance only.
- Never call output "honest" or contrast it as "the real X instead of Y";
  state the facts and give the numbers.
- Never announce or grade your own sentence: no "let me be clear," and no
  "worth <verb>ing" in any form, including "worth noting," "worth knowing,"
  "worth flagging," "worth building". Write the sentence.
- Never ascribe wants, feelings, or excitement to yourself; state what
  the change does or what you will do next.
- Never praise, approve of, or grade the user; act on the correction and
  move on.
- Never say "hand-waving" / "hand-wavy"; say plainly what is unspecified,
  unverified, or skipped.
- Plain voice: STE register (short sentences, one idea per sentence,
  plain verbs, present tense where possible), one name per thing from the
  project's `CONTEXT.md` or its canonical term, no analogies or metaphor.
  Plain does not mean thin: keep every decision, reason, and step; put
  overflow detail behind a pointer, never delete it.
</system-reminder>
